2.2
Miscellaneous preliminaries

We consign to this subsection various elementary miscellany about parametrised categories that we shall need for main body of this article. As such, this subsection may be safely skipped on first reading, to be returned to as needed.

Our first task is to record an “internal” version of the parametrised straightening–unstraightening equivalence, building upon the “external” version given in
[
BDG+16a
, Prop. 8.3]
. A similar, and much more general statement in the setting of categories parametrised over
\infty
–topoi, has already appeared as
[
Mar22
, Thm. 6.3.1]
. We only include the proof of
2.2.2
in our setup for the reader’s convenience.

To this end, first recall the notion of
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)cartesian fibrations from
[
Sha23
, Def. 7.1]
. For
\underline{S}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
, we will write
\mathrm{coCart}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{S})
for the category of
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocartesian fibrations over
\underline{S}
and morphisms the maps of
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocartesian fibrations.

Observation 2.2.1
.

In
[
Sha23
, Rem. 7.4]
it is stated that a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor
F\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocartesian fibration if and only if
\int F\colon\int\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\int\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is a cocartesian fibration in the usual sense. For our purposes in the next theorem, we would need a slightly more refined information in the form of a description of what the cocartesian lifts look like under these equivalent conditions, which we provide here. Write
p\colon\int\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
and
q\colon\int\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
for the structure cocartesian fibrations and let
f\colon x\rightarrow y
be a map in
\int\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
lying over
c\coloneqq q(f)\colon V\rightarrow W
in
{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
. We may then obtain a unique factorisation
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c^{*}x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{f}}

where
c^{*}x\in{\mathcal{D}}_{W}
,
u\colon x\rightarrow c^{*}x
is the
q
–cocartesian morphism over
c
, and
q(\overline{f})\simeq\mathrm{id}_{W}
. The claim now is that: (i) the
F_{W}
–cocartesian lift of
\overline{f}
is already a
\int F
–cocartesian lift; (ii) any
\int F
–cocartesian lift of
f\colon x\rightarrow y
is given by the composite of the
\int F
–cocartesian lift of
u
and the
F_{W}
–cocartesian lift of
\overline{f}
. Part (i) is gotten by the proof of
[
Sha23
, Lem. 7.5]
– but now using also that the fibrewise cocartesian lifts are preserved under the pushforward functors associated to morphisms in
{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
by the definition of
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocartesian fibrations. Combining (i) with the dual of
[
Lan21
, Lem. 3.1.7]
then yields part (ii) of the claim. Under this concrete elaboration of
[
Sha23
, Rmk. 7.4]
and since compositions of cocartesian fibrations are cocartesian fibrations by
[
Lan21
, Lem. 3.1.4]
, we see that the datum of a map of cocartesian fibrations over
\int\underline{S}
gives precisely the datum of a
{\mathcal{T}}
–map of
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocartesian fibrations over
\underline{S}
upon postcomposing with
\int\underline{S}\rightarrow{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
. Here we have also used that
F\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is a map of
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories (i.e.
\int F
is a map of
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocartesian fibrations) if and only if the
\int F
–cocartesian lift of all such
u
coming from a map in
{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
as above is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocartesian lift, again by an application of
[
Lan21
, Lem. 3.1.4]
.

Theorem 2.2.2

(Parametrised straightening/unstraightening)
.

Let
\underline{S}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. There is a natural equivalence
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{S},\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}})\simeq\mathrm{coCart}(\int\underline{S})\simeq\mathrm{coCart}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{S})
.

Proof.

We already know the first equivalence by
[
BDG+16a
, Prop. 8.3]
. To see the second equivalence, we write
p\colon\int\underline{S}\rightarrow{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
for the structure map. This map induces a functor
\mathrm{Cat}_{/\int\underline{S}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}_{/{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}}
which in turn factors through an adjunction

p\colon\mathrm{Cat}_{/\int\underline{S}}\rightleftharpoons(\mathrm{Cat}_{/{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}})_{/p}:\forget

which is an equivalence, where
\forget
forgets the map to
{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
. That this is an equivalence is standard, and can for example be seen by computing explicitly that
p
induces equivalences on the mapping spaces, and that it is clearly seen to be essentially surjective. Next, recall that we had non–full subcategories
\mathrm{coCart}(\int\underline{S})\subset\mathrm{Cat}_{/\int\underline{S}}
and
\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\simeq\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})\subset\mathrm{Cat}_{/{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}}
. In particular, by the usual straightening–unstraightening equivalence, we have the non–full subcategories
\mathrm{coCart}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{S})\subset(\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}})_{/\underline{S}}\subset(\mathrm{Cat}_{/{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}})_{/p}
. Now consider the solid diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}_{/\int\underline{S}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathrm{Cat}_{/{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}})_{/p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{coCart}(\int\underline{S})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{coCart}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{S})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\forget}

Our goal is to show that we have the dashed factorisations giving inverse equivalences. Since both non–full subcategories contain all equivalences, it would suffice to show that
p
and
\forget
admit such factorisations since then the natural equivalences
p\circ\forget\simeq\mathrm{id}
and
\forget\circ p\simeq\mathrm{id}
are also contained in the non–full subcategories. Since factoring through subcategories is a property of a functor that can be checked on objects and morphisms, the desired factorisations are now easy consequences of the concrete description of the cocartesian edges from
2.2.1
. This completes the proof of the theorem.
∎

Construction 2.2.3
.

2.2.2
. To describe this, first note by an easy inspection of

, Def. 7.1]

Notation 2.2.4
.

We write
\underline{\rfunc}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
(resp.
\underline{\lfunc}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
) for the
{\mathcal{T}}
-full subcategories of
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
consisting of
{\mathcal{T}}
-right adjoint functors (resp.
{\mathcal{T}}
-left adjoint functors); we write
\underline{\func}^{R}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
(resp.
\underline{\func}^{L}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
) for the
{\mathcal{T}}
-full subcategories of
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
consisting of strongly
{\mathcal{T}}
-limit-preserving functors (resp. strongly
{\mathcal{T}}
-colimit-preserving functors).

Next, we now record several facts about Beck–Chevalley (i.e. adjointed) squares.

Lemma 2.2.6
.

Suppose we have
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjunctions
L\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightleftharpoons\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:R
and
\widetilde{L}\colon\widetilde{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}\rightleftharpoons\widetilde{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}:\widetilde{R}
with adjunction (co)units
\eta,\varepsilon
and
\widetilde{\eta},\widetilde{{\varepsilon}}
respectively, together with a right adjointable square
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{L}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}}

For every
X\in\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
, we then have a natural identification of
\varphi\eta_{X}\colon\varphi X\rightarrow\varphi RLX
with
\widetilde{\eta}_{\varphi X}\colon\varphi X\rightarrow\widetilde{R}\widetilde{L}\varphi X
via the identification
\varphi RLX\simeq\widetilde{R}\widetilde{L}\varphi X
coming from adjointability. Similarly, for
A\in\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
, we have a natural identification of
\psi\varepsilon_{A}\colon\psi LRA\rightarrow\psi A
with
\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\psi A}\colon\widetilde{L}\widetilde{R}\psi A\rightarrow\psi A
.

Proof.

Recall that adjointability means the canonical Beck–Chevalley transformation

\varphi RY\xlongrightarrow{\widetilde{\eta}_{\varphi RY}}\widetilde{R}\widetilde{L}\varphi RY\simeq_{\widetilde{R}\sigma_{R}}\widetilde{R}\psi LRY\xlongrightarrow{\widetilde{R}\psi\varepsilon_{Y}}\widetilde{R}\psi Y

is an equivalence, where
\sigma
is the datum of the commutation
\psi L\simeq\widetilde{L}\varphi
. Hence, to prove the proposition, it would suffice to show that the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\widetilde{L}\varphi X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi RLX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\widetilde{L}\varphi RLX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\psi LRLX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\psi LX}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\eta}_{\varphi X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi\eta_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\eta}_{\varphi RLX}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\sigma_{RLX}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\psi\varepsilon_{LX}}

(7)

commutes. To this end, just observe that the bottom left composite participates in the following commuting diagram (where the bottom composite is an equivalence by adjointability)
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\widetilde{L}\varphi X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\psi LX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi RLX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\widetilde{L}\varphi RLX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\psi LRLX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\psi LX}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi\eta_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\eta}_{\varphi X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\widetilde{L}\varphi\eta_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\sigma_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\psi L\eta_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\eta}_{\varphi RLX}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\sigma_{RLX}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{R}\psi\varepsilon_{LX}}

yielding the desired commutation
Eq.

7
. The case of counits is similar, using instead the commuting diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{L}\varphi RA}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi LRA}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{L}\varphi RA}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{L}\widetilde{R}\widetilde{L}\varphi RA}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{L}\widetilde{R}\psi LRA}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{L}\widetilde{R}\psi A}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma_{RA}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi\varepsilon_{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{L}\widetilde{\eta}_{\varphi RA}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\widetilde{L}\varphi RA}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{L}\widetilde{R}\sigma_{RA}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\psi LRA}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{L}\widetilde{R}\psi\varepsilon_{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\psi A}}

where the bottom composite is the Beck–Chevalley equivalence.
∎

Proposition 2.2.7
.

Fix a category
J
and suppose we have two objects
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\in\func(J^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
together with a morphism
R\colon\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. Suppose moreover that the map
R
is fibrewise a right adjoint and that for each morphism
f\colon i\rightarrow j
in
J
, the Beck–Chevalley transformation
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}_{j}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}_{j}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Leftarrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{j}}

is an equivalence, where
L_{i}\dashv R_{i},L_{j}\dashv R_{j}
. Then the left adjoints assemble to a morphism
L\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
in
\func(J^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
which furthermore induces an adjunction in
\mathrm{Cat}

\lim_{J^{\mathrm{op}}}L\colon\lim_{J^{\mathrm{op}}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightleftharpoons\lim_{J^{\mathrm{op}}}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:\lim_{J^{\mathrm{op}}}R

Proof.

For the first part, we will use Lurie’s theory of relative adjunctions. Write
\int\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\int\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow J^{\mathrm{op}}
for the respective cocartesian unstraightening, so that we have a map of
J^{\mathrm{op}}
–cocartesian fibrations
R\colon\int\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\int\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. There are two conditions in
[
Lur17
, Prop. 7.3.2.11]
to check in order to obtain a left adjoint
L\colon\int\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\int\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
to
R
relative to
J^{\mathrm{op}}
. Condition (1) there is immediate from our fibrewise adjunction hypothesis. A straightforward unwinding of condition (2) there states that we need to check the following: for every morphism
f\colon i\rightarrow j
, the map
f^{*}\xrightarrow{f^{*}\eta}f^{*}R_{i}L_{i}\simeq R_{j}f^{*}L_{i}
adjoints to an equivalence
L_{j}f^{*}\xrightarrow{\simeq}f^{*}L_{i}
. But this adjointed map is precisely the Beck–Chevalley transformation, and so by hypothesis, is an equivalence. It is then an easy check to see that the relative left adjoint
L
is automatically a map of
J^{\mathrm{op}}
–cocartesian fibrations (see for example
[
Hil22a
, Prop. 2.2.5 (2)]
), whence a map
L\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
in
\func(J^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})\simeq\mathrm{coCart}(J^{\mathrm{op}})
as wanted. Finally, by the formula for limits in
\mathrm{Cat}
in terms of cocartesian sections of the cocartesian unstraightening (cf. the dual of
[
Lur09
, Cor. 3.3.3.2]
recorded for example in
[
HW21
, Prop. I.36]
), we obtain the adjunction

\lim_{J^{\mathrm{op}}}L\colon\lim_{J^{\mathrm{op}}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\simeq\Gamma_{\mathrm{cocart}}(\int\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightleftharpoons\Gamma_{\mathrm{cocart}}(\int\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\simeq\lim_{J^{\mathrm{op}}}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:\lim_{J^{\mathrm{op}}}R

as claimed.
∎

Fact 2.2.8

(Adjoints of equivariant functors)
.

It is a standard categorical fact that the
G
–equivariant structure of a functor admitting an adjoint induces a
G
–equivariant structure on the adjoint and on the adjunction. Since we have not been able to find it anywhere in the literature, we will record a proof of this here which we learnt from Maxime Ramzi. Let
L\colon{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{D}}
be a
G
–equivariant functor whose underlying functor admits a right adjoint. In particular,
L
can be encoded as a morphism in
\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})
and so upon unstraightening, we have a map
L\colon\int{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow\int{\mathcal{D}}
of cocartesian fibrations over
BG
. Now since
BG
was an
\infty
–groupoid, we get by
[
Lan21
, Lem. 3.1.6]
that all cocartesian morphisms in
\int{\mathcal{C}}
and
\int{\mathcal{D}}
are equivalences. In particular, any map between them over
BG
is a map of cocartesian fibrations. Hence, by the dual of
[
Lur17
, Prop. 7.3.2.11]
, the fibrewise right adjoint coming from the underlying adjunction induces a relative right adjoint
R\colon\int{\mathcal{D}}\rightarrow\int{\mathcal{C}}
which is automatically a map of cocartesian fibrations over
BG
by the previous sentence. All in all, we have obtained a
G
–equivariant structure on the right adjoint as well as on the unit and counit maps, as wanted.

The next pair of results provide abstract colimit decomposition results that will be crucial to our cubical theory in
Section

3
.

Lemma 2.2.9
.

Suppose we are given a map
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathcal{A}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathcal{A}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathcal{A}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q^{*}}

of diagrams in
\func(\Lambda^{2}_{0},\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}})
, where
\gamma^{*},\beta^{*},p^{*},q^{*},r^{*}
admit right adjoints
\gamma_{*},\beta_{*},p_{*},q_{*},r_{*}
respectively. If
\underline{\mathcal{A}}
has pullbacks, then the functor
p^{*}\times_{r^{*}}q^{*}\colon\underline{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{\underline{\mathcal{E}}}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
has a right adjoint given by the functor
\varphi
sending
(c,d)\in\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{\underline{\mathcal{E}}}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
to the pullback in
\underline{\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi(c,d)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{*}d}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{*}c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{*}\gamma^{*}c\simeq r_{*}\beta^{*}d}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{*}\eta^{\beta}_{d}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{*}\eta^{\gamma}_{c}}

Similarly, if
\gamma^{*},\beta^{*},p^{*},q^{*},r^{*}
admit instead left adjoints
\gamma_{!},\beta_{!},p_{!},q_{!},r_{!}
respectively and
\underline{\mathcal{A}}
admits pushouts, then the functor
p^{*}\times_{r^{*}}q^{*}
admits a left adjoint given by the functor
\psi
sending
(c,d)\in\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{\underline{\mathcal{E}}}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
to the pushout in
\underline{\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{!}\gamma^{*}c\simeq r_{!}\beta^{*}d}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{!}d}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{!}c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi(c,d)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{!}\varepsilon^{\beta}_{d}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{!}\varepsilon^{\gamma}_{c}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}

Proof.

The putative right adjoint
\varphi
is clearly a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor, and is fibrewise a right adjoint by
[
HY17
, Thm. 5.5]
. Hence, by
2.1.13
, we get that
\varphi
is indeed the
{\mathcal{T}}
–right adjoint of
p^{*}\times_{r^{*}}q^{*}
. The statement for the left adjoint follows by passing to the opposite categories.
∎

Corollary 2.2.10
.

Suppose we have a pushout diagram in
\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathcal{B}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathcal{P}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}

and let
\underline{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
have all
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits. Then for any
\partial\in\underline{\func}(\underline{\mathcal{P}},\underline{\mathcal{A}})
, we have the following pushout diagram in
\underline{\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{\mathcal{B}}}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{\mathcal{P}}}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}

where we have suppressed the restriction functors. A similar statement holds for limits, with all colimits in sight replaced with limits.

Proof.

This is an immediate consequence of
2.2.9
, using that
\underline{\func}(\underline{\mathcal{P}},\underline{\mathcal{A}})\simeq\underline{\func}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\mathcal{A}})\times_{\underline{\func}(\underline{\mathcal{B}},\underline{\mathcal{A}})}\underline{\func}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},\underline{\mathcal{A}})
by definition of
\underline{\mathcal{P}}
as a pushout.
∎

Next, recall the notion of
{\mathcal{T}}
–faithful functors from
[
Hil22a
, Def. 3.4.4]
, i.e. a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor which induces fibrewise inclusions of components on mapping spaces.

Lemma 2.2.11
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subset\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–faithful inclusion where
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is closed under limits of shape
\underline{J}
. Then
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
inherits
\underline{J}
–shaped limits from
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
if the following conditions hold:

1.

for any object
\partial\in\underline{\func}(\underline{J},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\subset\underline{\func}(\underline{J},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
, the limit of
\partial
has the property of lying in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
and the adjunction counit
\underline{\operatorname{const}}_{\underline{J}}\underline{\lim}_{\underline{J}}\partial\rightarrow\partial
lies in
\underline{\func}(\underline{J},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
,

2.

for any
C\in\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
equipped with a morphism
\underline{\operatorname{const}}_{\underline{J}}C\rightarrow\partial
in
\underline{\func}(\underline{J},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
, the induced morphism
C\rightarrow\underline{\lim}_{\underline{J}}\partial
lies in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subset\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
.

A similar statement holds also for colimits by passing to the opposite categories.

Proof.

Suppose we are given such an object
\partial\in\underline{\func}(\underline{J},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
satisfying (1) and (2). We need to argue that the natural map
\mathchoice{\mbox{\uline{\phantom{$\displaystyle\map$}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.0pt\raisebox{0.5pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.19133pt\raisebox{0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.35355pt\raisebox{0.35355pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.46193pt\raisebox{0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.5pt\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.46193pt\raisebox{-0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.35355pt\raisebox{-0.35355pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.19133pt\raisebox{-0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.0pt\raisebox{-0.5pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.19133pt\raisebox{-0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.35355pt\raisebox{-0.35355pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.46193pt\raisebox{-0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.5pt\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.19133pt\raisebox{0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\mbox{$\displaystyle\map$}}}}{\mbox{\uline{\phantom{$\textstyle\map$}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.0pt\raisebox{0.5pt}[0.0pt]{$\textstyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.19133pt\raisebox{0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\textstyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip where the bottom horizontal is an equivalence by definition of
\underline{\lim}_{\underline{J}}\partial
. Since the vertical maps are inclusion of subcomponents, so is the top horizontal map. Hence, we are left to showing that the top horizontal map is
\pi_{0}
–surjective, which is precisely supplied by condition (2).
∎

We include the proof of the following standard observation for the reader’s convenience as well as to establish what we mean by “reflecting (co)limits”.

Lemma 2.2.12
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},\underline{I},\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
such that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
admits
\underline{I}
–shaped (co)limits. Let
F\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
be a conservative functor preserving
\underline{I}
–shaped (co)limits. Then
F
reflects
\underline{I}
–shaped (co)limits.

Proof.

Without loss of generality we deal with the case of limits. Suppose we have a coned
\underline{I}
–shaped diagram
\partial\colon\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleleft}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
such that
F\partial\colon\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleleft}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is a limit diagram. This means that if we write
\infty
for the cone point, then we have a map
\partial(\infty)\rightarrow\underline{\lim}_{\underline{I}}\partial
in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
such that
F\partial(\infty)\rightarrow F\underline{\lim}_{\underline{I}}\partial\simeq\underline{\lim}_{\underline{I}}F\partial
is an equivalence in
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
. Since
F
was conservative, we get that
\partial(\infty)\rightarrow\underline{\lim}_{\underline{I}}\partial
was already an equivalence, as was to be shown.
∎

We will deduce the parametrised analogue of
[
MP87
, Lem 1.7.ii]
from the unparametrised version proven in
[
CDH+
]
. We will need some terminology for this.

Terminology 2.2.13
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-cocomplete category and
S
be a set of objects in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. We say that it is
jointly conservative
if
S
induces a jointly conservative set of objects in each fibre of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
, i.e. for every
V\in{{\mathcal{T}}}
and writing
S_{V}
for the set of objects of
{\mathcal{C}}_{V}
in the set
S
, the functor
\prod_{x\in S_{V}}\map_{{\mathcal{C}}_{V}}(x,-):{\mathcal{C}}_{V}\rightarrow\prod_{x\in S_{V}}\mathcal{S}
is conservative. We say that it is a
set of parametrised generators of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
if the smallest
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-cocomplete subcategory of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
containing
S
is
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
itself. That is, every parametrised object in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
can be written as a parametrised colimit of objects in
S
.

Now recall the notion of parametrised compactness from the paragraph before
2.1.34
.

Proposition 2.2.14

(Parametrised Makkai-Pitts)
.

Let
\kappa
be a regular cardinal and
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
a
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-cocomplete category. Let
S\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a jointly conservative set of parametrised-
\kappa
-compact objects. Then
S
is a set of parametrised-
\kappa
-compact generators. In particular,
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is parametrised-
\kappa
-compactly generated.

Proof.

We want to show that for every
V\in{{\mathcal{T}}}
, any
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–object in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}}
is a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–colimit of objects in
S
. By hypothesis,
\prod_{x\in S_{V}}\map_{{\mathcal{C}}_{V}}(x,-)\colon{\mathcal{C}}_{V}\rightarrow\prod_{x\in S_{V}}\mathcal{S}
is jointly conservative. Hence, by
[
CDH+
, Prop 1.1.2]
, every object in
{\mathcal{C}}_{V}
is a
\kappa
-small colimit of objects in
S_{V}
.
∎

Proof.

This is just the proof of
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.5.3.3]
written in our setting, except that we do not need to invoke the adjoint functor
2.1.35
since
\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{L}
and
\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{R}
were defined with morphisms being left and right adjoints respectively. Write
\widehat{\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
and
\underline{\mathrm{CAT}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
for the
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories of large and huge
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories, respectively. In particular, we have that
\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{L},\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{R}\subset\widehat{\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\in\underline{\mathrm{CAT}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. Now, fix a
\underline{S}\in\underline{\mathrm{CAT}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. Under the cocartesian unstraightening equivalence of
2.2.2
, it is easy to see that elements in
\pi_{0}\map_{{\mathrm{CAT}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}}(\underline{S},\underline{\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}}_{{\mathcal{T}}})
that lie in
\pi_{0}\map_{{\mathrm{CAT}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}}(\underline{S},\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{L})\subset\pi_{0}\map_{{\mathrm{CAT}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}}(\underline{S},\underline{\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}}_{{\mathcal{T}}})
are precisely those
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocartesian fibrations
\underline{\mathcal{P}}\rightarrow\underline{S}
which are also
{\mathcal{T}}
–cartesian and whose parametrised fibres are
{\mathcal{T}}
–presentable. Similarly, under the cartesian unstraightening from
2.2.3

, it suffices just to prove the case of presheaves in spaces. Let
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\in\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{{\mathcal{T}}_{/W}}
. By
[
Nar17
, Prop. 3.19]
, the restriction map
\underline{\func}^{L}_{W}\big(f_{\otimes}\underline{\presheaf}_{U}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}),\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\big)\longrightarrow\underline{\func}_{W}\big(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\big)
is an equivalence. But then the target is naturally equivalent to
\underline{\func}^{L}_{W}\big(\underline{\presheaf}_{W}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}),\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\big)
by
[
Sha23
, Thm. 11.5]
and so we are done.
∎

Observation 2.2.21

(
{\mathcal{T}}
–exactness on
{\mathcal{T}}
–stables)
.

Write
\underline{\func}^{{\mathrm{lex}}},\underline{\func}^{{\mathrm{rex}}},\underline{\func}^{{\mathrm{ex}}}\subseteq\underline{\func}
for the full subcategories of functors which preserve finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits, finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits, and finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)limits, respectively.
If
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
are
{\mathcal{T}}
–stable, then note that the two
{\mathcal{T}}
–full subcategories
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{lex}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\subseteq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\supseteq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{rex}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
agree. To wit, both imply that they are fibrewise right and left exact (since these are fibrewise stable after all); moreover, preserving finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts and preserving finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–products are equivalent since
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
were
{\mathcal{T}}
–semiadditive. Hence in this case we have
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{lex}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})=\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{ex}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})=\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{rex}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
.

Lemma 2.2.22
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
have finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits and
\underline{\mathcal{A}}
admit finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits. Then we have a canonical equivalence
\underline{\func}^{{\mathrm{lex}}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{A}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))\simeq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{A}},\underline{\func}^{{\mathrm{lex}}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))
.

Proof.

Note that we have the identification

\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{A}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))\simeq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{A}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))
since
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits of functor categories are computed in the target by
[
Hil22a
, Prop. 3.1.12]
. To see that we have the desired equivalence, consider the diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}^{{\mathrm{lex}}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{A}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{A}},\underline{\func}^{{\mathrm{lex}}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{A}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{A}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

That the bottom arrows restrict to the dashed arrows is because again by
[
Hil22a
, Prop. 3.1.12]
,
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits in both
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{A}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
and
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{lex}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
are computed in
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
.
∎

Proof.

That it is small is clear. To see that it is
{\mathcal{T}}
–stable, just note

\begin{split}\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{ex}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})&\simeq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{lex}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\\
&\simeq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{lex}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{S}}_{*{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{fin}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))\\
&\simeq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{S}}_{*{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{fin}}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{lex}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))\\
&\simeq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{lin}}(\underline{\mathcal{S}}_{*{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{fin}}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{ex}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))\end{split}

where the first and last equivalences are by
2.2.21
, the second is by
[
Nar16
, Thm. 7.4]
, and the third by
2.2.22
. Hence, by
[
Nar16
, Thm. 7.4]
again, we see that
\underline{\func}^{\mathrm{ex}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–stable. For
{\mathcal{T}}
–idempotent-completeness, note that
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits of
\underline{\func}^{{\mathrm{ex}}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\simeq\underline{\func}^{{\mathrm{rex}}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
are computed in
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
, and since being
{\mathcal{T}}
–idempotent-complete is just the condition of admitting certain fibrewise
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits, this point is clear too.
∎

∎

2.3
Symmetric monoidality and localisations

Convention:
From now on for the rest of the article, our base category
{\mathcal{T}}
will always be assumed to be atomic orbital.

The main aim of this subsection is to give a multiplicative enhancement of the presentable Dwyer–Kan localisations from
[
Hil22a
,
\lx@sectionsign 6.3
]
.

Terminology 2.3.1
.

Let
S
be a collection of morphisms in a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. For any
U=U_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup U_{n}\in\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
where
U_{i}\in{\mathcal{T}}
, we will write
S_{U}
for the collection of morphisms inside
S
in
{\mathcal{C}}_{U}\simeq{\mathcal{C}}_{U_{1}}\times\cdots\times{\mathcal{C}}_{U_{n}}
. We will say that
S
is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–
collection
if for any morphism
f\colon U\rightarrow V
in
\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
and any morphism
\varphi\colon A\rightarrow B
in
S_{V}
(in general, this is a tuple of morphisms as is clear from our definition of
S_{V}
in the preceding sentence), the morphism
f^{*}\varphi\colon f^{*}A\rightarrow f^{*}B
is a morphism in
S_{U}
.

Terminology 2.3.2
.

We say that a
{\mathcal{T}}
–collection of morphisms
S
in a
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal category
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
is
\underline{\otimes}
–multiplicatively closed
if for any
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
, any morphism
p\colon U\rightarrow V
in
\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
, and any morphism
\varphi\colon A\rightarrow B
in
S_{U}
, the morphism
p_{\otimes}\varphi\colon p_{\otimes}A\rightarrow p_{\otimes}B
in
{\mathcal{C}}_{V}
lies in
S_{V}
.

Notation 2.3.3
.

We recall the clarifying distinction between
Dwyer-Kan localisations
and
Bousfield localisations
due to
[
Hin16
]
, which we have also adopted in
[
Hil22a
]
. By
{{\mathcal{T}}}
–Dwyer–Kan localisations, we will mean the following: let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-category and
S
a
{\mathcal{T}}
–collection of morphisms in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. Suppose now that a
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-category
S^{-1}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
exists and is equipped with a map
\mathrm{DK}:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow S^{-1}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
inducing the equivalence

{\mathrm{DK}}^{*}:\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(S^{-1}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\xrightarrow{\simeq}\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{S^{-1}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})

for all
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-categories
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
, where
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{S^{-1}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\subseteq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
is the
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-full subcategory of parametrised functors sending morphisms in
S
to equivalences. If such a
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-category exists, then it must necessarily be unique, and this is then defined to be the
{{\mathcal{T}}}
–Dwyer–Kan localisation of

\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}

with respect to

S
.

By
{{\mathcal{T}}}
–Bousfield localisations
, we mean a
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-adjunction
L:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightleftarrows\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:i
where the
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-right adjoint
i
is
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-fully faithful. Writing
Z
for the morphisms in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
that get sent to equivalences under
L
, we may then view
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
as precisely the
{\mathcal{T}}
–full subcategory of
Z
–local objects
, i.e. those
X\in\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
such that for any morphism
\varphi\colon A\rightarrow B
in
Z
, the induced map

Proposition 2.3.4

(Dwyer-Kan symmetric monoidality)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal category and
S
a
{\mathcal{T}}
–collection of morphisms in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
which is
\underline{\otimes}
–multiplicatively closed. Then:

1.

the Dwyer–Kan localisation
S^{-1}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
attains a unique
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal structure such that the canonical map
\mathrm{DK}\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow S^{-1}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
enhances to a
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal functor,

is an equivalence.

Proof.

The proof will proceed by bootstrapping from the construction and proof of
[
Lur17
, Prop. 4.1.7.4]
. Recall from
[
Lur17
, Cons. 4.1.7.1]
that we have a category
\mathrm{WCat}
whose objects are pairs
({\mathcal{C}},W)
where
{\mathcal{C}}
is a category and
W
is a collection of morphisms in
{\mathcal{C}}
stable under composition and contains all equivalences in
{\mathcal{C}}
, and morphisms
f:({\mathcal{C}},W)\rightarrow({\mathcal{C}}^{\prime},W^{\prime})
are functors
f:{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime}
such that
f(W)\subseteq W^{\prime}
. By
[
Lur17
, Prop. 4.1.7.2]
we have a Bousfield localisation

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{WCat}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I}

(8)

where both functors preserve finite products and the functor
I
sends
({\mathcal{C}},W)
to the Dwyer-Kan localisation
W^{-1}{\mathcal{C}}
. Applying
2.1.5
to this adjunction we get the
{\mathcal{T}}
–Bousfield localisation
\underline{I}_{{\mathcal{T}}}:\cofree_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathrm{WCat})\rightleftarrows\cofree_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathrm{Cat}):\underline{\mathrm{incl}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. Moreover, since both functors in
Eq.

8
preserve finite products, the functor
\underline{I}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
preserves indexed products. Hence, applying the forgetful functor from
2.1.27
, we even have a commuting square of
{\mathcal{T}}
–Bousfield localisations

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\cmonoid}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathrm{WCat})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\cmonoid}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathrm{Cat})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cofree_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathrm{WCat})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cofree_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathrm{Cat})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{I}_{T}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\forget}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathrm{incl}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\forget}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{I}_{T}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathrm{incl}}}

(9)

It is straightforward to see that our hypotheses on the pair
(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},S)\in\cofree_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathrm{WCat})
ensures that it lifts to an object in
\underline{\cmonoid}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathrm{WCat})
. Furthermore, recall that
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal categories are equivalently
{\mathcal{T}}
–commutative monoids in
\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
by
2.1.32
(1).

Given these, part (1) may now be obtained exactly by the argument in
[
GGN15
, Lem. 3.6]
(which also saw an immediate parametrised adaptation in
[
Hil22a
, Lem. 4.2.3]
). For part (2), we would like to argue that for any
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\underline{\mathcal{E}}

Remark 2.3.5
.

For our multiplicative considerations shortly, the following notations and observations will be important. For a
{\mathcal{T}}
–collection of morphisms
S
in a
{\mathcal{T}}
–presentable category
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
, we write
S_{\underline{\amalg}}\supseteq S
for the closure of
S
under finite indexed coproducts of morphisms in
S
. Similarly, we denote by
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}\supseteq S_{\underline{\amalg}}\supseteq S
the closure of
S
under
all
parametrised colimits valued in
S
. These are easily seen to be, again,
{\mathcal{T}}
–collections of morphisms. We write
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}^{-1}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},S_{\underline{\amalg}}^{-1}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
for the
{\mathcal{T}}
–full subcategories of
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}
– and
S_{\underline{\amalg}}
–local objects in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
respectively (this is consistent with
2.3.3
by virtue of
[
Hil22a
, Thm. 6.3.7]
). Since
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}\supseteq S_{\underline{\amalg}}
, we have the inclusion
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}^{-1}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subseteq S_{\underline{\amalg}}^{-1}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. To see that this inclusion is an equivalence, let
X\in S^{-1}_{\underline{\amalg}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
and let
\partial\colon\underline{J}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\Delta^{1}}
be a diagram taking values in
S
. We need to show that
X
is local against the morphism
\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}}\colon\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}}\partial_{0}\rightarrow\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}}\partial_{1}
in
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}
. But this is clearly implied by the commutation

to0.0pt{\hskip-0.19133pt\raisebox{0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\scriptscriptstyle\map$}\hss}\mbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\map$}}}}(\partial_{1},X)
and the analogous ones for
\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}}\partial_{0}
and
\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}}\partial
.

Lemma 2.3.6
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–presentable category equipped with a
{\mathcal{T}}
–distributive–symmetric–monoidal structure
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
. Let
S
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–collection of morphisms in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
and
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}\supseteq S
its closure from
2.3.5
. If
S
is
\underline{\otimes}
–multiplicatively closed, then so is
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}
.

Proof.

Let
p\colon W\rightarrow U
be a morphism in
\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
and suppose we have a diagram of morphisms
\partial\colon\underline{J}\rightarrow p^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\Delta^{1}}
in
S
. Our goal is to show that the morphism
p_{\otimes}\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}}\partial
is still contained in
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}
. By
{\mathcal{T}}
–distributivity, we have the equivalence

p_{\otimes}\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}}\partial\simeq\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}\big(p_{*}\underline{J}\xlongrightarrow{p_{*}\partial}p_{*}p^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\Delta^{1}}\xlongrightarrow{p_{\otimes}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\Delta^{1}}\big)

where we have endowed
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\Delta^{1}}
with the pointwise
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal structure from
[
NS22
,
\lx@sectionsign 3.3
]
, which is again
{\mathcal{T}}
–distributive. Since
S
is
\underline{\otimes}
–multiplicatively closed, the right hand side is in
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}
, and so
p_{\otimes}\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}}\partial
is too, as required.
∎

Proposition 2.3.7
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–presentable category equipped with a
{\mathcal{T}}
–distributive–symmetric–monoidal structure
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
. Let
S
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–collection of morphisms in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
.

1.

There is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–presentable category
L_{S}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
participating in a
{\mathcal{T}}
–Bousfield localisation
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{S}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}:i}

satisfying the following universal property: for any other
{\mathcal{T}}
–presentable category
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
, the map
L
induces the equivalence

L^{*}\colon\underline{\func}^{L}(L_{S}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\xlongrightarrow{\simeq}\underline{\func}^{L,S^{-1}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
.

2.

If
S
was furthermore
\underline{\otimes}
–multiplicatively closed, then there is a canonical enhancement
L_{S}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
of
L_{S}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
to the structure of a
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal category. This is uniquely characterised by the following universal property: for any
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal category
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
, this functor induces the equivalence
L^{*}\colon\underline{\func}^{\underline{\otimes},L}(L_{S}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\xlongrightarrow{\simeq}\underline{\func}^{\underline{\otimes},L,S^{-1}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
.

Proof.

Part (1) is an immediate consequence of
[
Hil22a
, Thm. 6.3.7]
, using
L_{S}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\coloneqq S^{-1}_{\underline{\amalg}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. For part (2), we recall that
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}^{-1}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\simeq S^{-1}_{\underline{\amalg}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
from
2.3.5
. Now,
2.3.6
ensures that
S_{\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}}
is
\underline{\otimes}
–multiplicatively closed, and so by
2.3.4
(1) we obtain the first sentence of (2). The final sentence is now an immediate combination of the universal property of part (1) and
2.3.4
(2).
∎

2.4
Borel equivariant theory

In this subsection, we specialise for the moment to the case of
{\mathcal{T}}=\mathcal{O}_{G}
. We write
b\colon BG\hookrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{G}
for the fully faithful inclusion of the free transitive
G
–set
G/e
. This subsection pertains to working out some far–reaching consequences of constructions associated to this one map just from adjunction considerations. The philosophy here is to seriously reckon with the fact that the process of forgetting “genuine”
G
–structures to “Borel”
G
–structures is one that penetrates and appears on multiple categorical levels. In this sense, the “categorification–decategorification” approach we present here is very much in line with the so–called “metacosm–macrocosm–microcosm” trichotomy of
[
AMR22
]
. Our end point will be the full version of
A
in the form of
2.4.10
and our starting point is the Bousfield localisation

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}\colon\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}=\func(\mathcal{O}_{G}^{\mathrm{op}},\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(BG,\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}):b_{*}}

(10)

The
G
–category of small
G
–categories
\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}
is then an object of
\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}
. Due to its special role throughout, we denote
b_{*}b^{*}\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}\in\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}
by
\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat})
for
Borel
G
–categories
. By the right Kan extension formula, we see that under the embedding
b_{*}
from
Eq.

10
,
\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat})
is the
G
–category whose value at
G/H
is given by
\mathrm{Cat}^{hH}\simeq\func(BH,\mathrm{Cat})
. Importantly, the adjunction unit
\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}\rightarrow\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat})
can be checked easily to be given precisely
again
by the map
b^{*}
. By right Kan extension, the
G
–functor
b^{*}\colon\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}\rightarrow\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat})
admits fibrewise fully faithful right adjoints
b_{*}
. Over every fibre, objects in
\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat})
may then be viewed via
b_{*}
precisely as those objects in
\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}
which are
Borel local
, i.e. those
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}
with the property that if
\varphi\colon\underline{I}\rightarrow\underline{J}
is a map in
\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}
such that
b^{*}\varphi
is an equivalence (such maps are also called Borel equivalences), then
\varphi^{*}\colon{\map}_{\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}}(\underline{J},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightarrow{\map}_{\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is an equivalence. Similarly,
b^{*}
also admits fibrewise fully faithful left adjoints
b_{!}
by left Kan extension. Under this inclusion,
\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat})
may be viewed as the
Borel colocal
objects, i.e. those
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}
such that
\varphi_{*}\colon{\map}_{\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{I})\rightarrow{\map}_{\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{J})
is an equivalence for any Borel equivalence
\varphi\colon\underline{I}\rightarrow\underline{J}
. The first observation to be made is that these can be assembled to a
G
–Bousfield (co)localisation by the following:

Proposition 2.4.1
.

The
G
–functor
b^{*}
participates in the
G
–Bousfield (co)localisation

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{!}}

Proof.

We would like to use
2.1.13
and its dual to say that the fibrewise fully faithful right/left adjoints assemble to a
G
–functor. For the case of
b_{*}
, without loss of generality, we show that for every
H\leq G
, the adjointed square
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}_{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}_{H}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(BH,\mathrm{Cat})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\res^{G}_{H}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Rightarrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\res^{G}_{H}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{*}}

commutes. To this end, we will use the Borel local description given above and we show the following: if
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
is Borel local, then
\res^{G}_{H}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{H}
is also Borel local. So let
\varphi\colon\underline{I}\rightarrow\underline{J}
be a Borel equivalence in
\mathrm{Cat}_{H}
. Since the functor
\forget\colon\func(BH,\mathrm{Cat})\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}
is conservative, this is the same as requiring that
\res^{H}_{e}\varphi
is an equivalence. The key point now is that because of this, and because
\res^{G}_{e}\coprod_{G/H}\simeq\coprod_{g\in G/H}\res^{H}_{e}
, we see that
\coprod_{G/H}\varphi\colon\coprod_{G/H}\underline{I}\rightarrow\coprod_{G/H}\underline{J}
is still a Borel equivalence. Hence, by the computation

\map_{\mathrm{Cat}_{H}}(\underline{J},\res^{G}_{H}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\simeq\map_{\mathrm{Cat}_{G}}(\coprod_{G/H}\underline{J},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\xrightarrow[\simeq]{\varphi^{*}}\map_{\mathrm{Cat}_{G}}(\coprod_{G/H}\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\simeq\map_{\mathrm{Cat}_{H}}(\underline{I},\res^{G}_{H}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})

we see that
\res^{G}_{H}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is still Borel local, as claimed. The case of
b_{!}
is similar, using now instead that
\res^{G}_{e}\prod_{G/H}\simeq\prod_{g\in G/H}\res^{H}_{e}
, so that
\prod_{G/H}\varphi
is still a Borel equivalence.
∎

In the rest of the article, by the word
Borelification
we will mean either the functor
b^{*}
or
b_{*}b^{*}
in all its various incarnations at various categorical levels.

Observation 2.4.2
.

A point that we will be using several times to prove properties relating to
b^{*}
is that it is the unique dashed lift
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}_{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\forget}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\res^{G}_{e}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}}

associated to the
G
–equivariant functor
\res^{G}_{e}
(with trivial
G
–equivariance everywhere).

Proposition 2.4.3

(Omnibus basics of Borelification)
.

Let
\underline{J}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
,
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}
and
{\mathcal{D}}\in\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat})
.

1.

There is a natural equivalence
b^{*}\underline{\func}(\underline{J},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\simeq\func(b^{*}\underline{J},b^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
of objects in
\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat})
,

2.

the adjunction unit
\underline{\func}(\underline{J},b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})\rightarrow b_{*}b^{*}\underline{\func}(\underline{J},b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})
is an equivalence,

3.

if
{\mathcal{D}}
has finite (co)products, then
b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
is a
G
–category with finite indexed (co)products. In the case of admitting products, we furthermore have a natural equivalence
\underline{\cmonoid}_{G}(b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})\simeq b_{*}\cmonoid({\mathcal{D}})
,

4.

if
{\mathcal{D}}
is moreover semiadditive as an object in
\mathrm{Cat}
, then
b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}\in{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}
is a
G
–semiadditive
G
–category.

Proof.

For part (1), note that we have both commuting squares
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}_{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}_{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\res^{G}_{e}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}(\underline{J},-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(\res^{G}_{e}\underline{J},-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(b^{*}\underline{J},-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\forget}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\forget}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\res^{G}_{e}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(\res^{G}_{e}\underline{J},-)}

Here, all categories and functors in the left square are endowed with the trivial
G
–equivariant structure. Hence, by
2.4.2
, the bottom left composite of the left square lifts to the functor
b^{*}\underline{\func}(\underline{J},-)\colon\mathrm{Cat}_{G}\rightarrow\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})
. On the other hand, the same observation together with the right commuting square yields that the unique lift to
\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})
of the top right composite of the left square is given by
\func(b^{*}\underline{J},b^{*}-)\colon\mathrm{Cat}_{G}\rightarrow\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})
. This gives part (1).

For part (2), we just need to show that
\underline{\func}(\underline{J},b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})
is Borel local, and this is an immediate consequence of the definition and unwinding adjunctions, using also the fact that
b^{*}
preserves products (for example because it has a left adjoint
b_{!}
).

For point (3), we deal with the case of products since that of coproducts will be dual. Let
H\leq G
and
w\colon G/H\rightarrow G/G
be the unique equivariant map. This then induces a
G
–equivariant map
w^{*}\colon{\mathcal{D}}\simeq\func(G/G,{\mathcal{D}})\rightarrow\func(G/H,{\mathcal{D}})\simeq\prod_{G/H}\res^{G}_{H}{\mathcal{D}}
. Since
{\mathcal{D}}
has finite products and since
w^{*}
was
G
–equivariant, this map admits a right adjoint
w_{*}
which furthermore can be endowed with a canonical
G
–equivariant structure with
G
–equivariant (co)units by
2.2.8
. In particular, this induces, upon applying
(-)^{hG}
, the adjunction
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})^{G}={\mathcal{D}}^{hG}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\prod_{G/H}\res^{G}_{H}{\mathcal{D}})^{hG}\simeq{\mathcal{D}}^{hH}=(w_{*}w^{*}b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})^{G}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w_{*}}

To see that this can be assembled to a
G
–adjunction
w^{*}\colon b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}\rightleftharpoons w_{*}w^{*}b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}:w_{*}
, we need to show by
2.1.13
that
w_{*}
commutes with restrictions under the appropriate Beck–Chevalley transformation. The key to this is the double coset decomposition of finite
G
–sets. More precisely, let
K\leq G
and
f\colon G/K\rightarrow G/G
. Then by the double coset decomposition we have the left pullback diagram of finite
G
–sets
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{g\in K\backslash G/H}G/K^{g}\cap H}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/H}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{g\in K\backslash G/H}\prod_{G/K^{g}\cap H}\res^{G}_{G/K^{g}\cap H}{\mathcal{D}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{G/H}\res^{G}_{H}{\mathcal{D}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/G}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{G/K}\res^{G}_{K}{\mathcal{D}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w_{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Leftarrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}

Applying
\func(-,{\mathcal{D}})
, we obtain the adjointed square on the right of
G
–equivariant maps and transformation, again by
2.2.8
. This commutes by
[
Lur17
, Lem. 6.1.6.3]
. Finally, applying
(-)^{hG}
to the right square gives us the commutation of the Beck–Chevalley square in the aforementioned criterion, as required.

For the second part of (3), since
\res^{G}_{e}\underline{\cmonoid}_{G}(b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})\simeq\cmonoid({\mathcal{D}})\in\mathrm{Cat}
, we see by the same argument as for part (1) that
b^{*}\underline{\cmonoid}_{G}(b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})\simeq\cmonoid({\mathcal{D}})\in\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})
. Hence, we need only to argue that
\underline{\cmonoid}_{G}(b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})
is Borel local. So let
\varphi\colon\underline{I}\rightarrow\underline{J}
be a Borel equivalence. Recall from
2.1.24
that
\underline{\cmonoid}_{G}(b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})\coloneqq\underline{\func}^{\mathrm{sadd}}(\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*},b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})
. Now, simply consider the natural equivalences

\underline{\func}(\underline{J},\underline{\func}^{\mathrm{sadd}}(\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*},b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}))\simeq\underline{\func}^{\mathrm{sadd}}(\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*},\underline{\func}(\underline{J},b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}))\simeq\underline{\func}^{\mathrm{sadd}}(\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*},b_{*}\func(b^{*}\underline{J},{\mathcal{D}}))

to conclude, where the second equivalence is by points (1) and (2).

Lastly, point (4) is simply because, as explained in the proof of part (3), the indexed (co)product for
b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}
are induced by the left and right adjoint of the
G
–equivariant restriction functor
{\mathcal{D}}\rightarrow\prod_{G/H}\res^{G}_{H}{\mathcal{D}}
. Hence, forgetting the
G
–equivariant structure on the
G
–semiadditivity norm map
Eq.

6
gives the usual semiadditivity norm map associated to the set of size
|G/H|
, which is an equivalence by hypothesis.
∎

Proposition 2.4.4
.

Applying the transformation
\forget\colon\underline{\cmonoid}_{G}(-)\rightarrow\mathrm{id}(-)
from
2.1.27
to the
b^{*}\dashv b_{*}

G
–Bousfield localisation of
2.4.1
yields the commuting square of
G
–Bousfield localisations (i.e. both the
(b^{*},\forget)
and
(b_{*},\forget)
squares commute)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}_{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\forget}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\forget}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{*}}

(11)

Proof.

By
b_{!}\dashv b^{*}\dashv b_{*}
from
2.4.1
, both
b^{*}
and
b_{*}
preserve finite indexed products. Since
\underline{\cmonoid}_{G}(-)
is functorial on finite indexed product–preserving functors and since the
\forget
transformation is implemented by precomposition from
2.1.27
, we immediately obtain a commuting square of
G
–Bousfield localisations. All that is left to argue is that
\underline{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat}))\simeq\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))
: this is precisely supplied by
2.4.3
(3).
∎

Remark 2.4.5
.

Recall that by definition,
\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Cat})\coloneqq\func^{\times}(\effBurn(G),\mathrm{Cat})
. It is then standard that we have
\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Cat})\simeq\mackey_{G}(\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))
: to wit, since
\effBurn(G)
is semiadditive by
[
Bar17
, Prop. 4.3, Ex. B]
, we may immediately deduce the fact for example from
[
HW21
, Thm. II.19]
. Evaluating the top horizontal
G
–adjunction from
Eq.

11
at
G/G
and using that
\cmonoid_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})\simeq\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Cat})
from
[
Nar16
, Thm. 6.5]
yields the Bousfield localisation

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}\colon\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Cat})\simeq\mackey_{G}(\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(BG,\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})):b_{*}}

This then recovers
[
BGS20
, Cons. 8.1]
, and one may indeed view
2.4.4
as a parametrised enhancement of the cited result.

Observation 2.4.6
.

Suppose we are given an object
{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}\in\func(BG,\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))
. Then by
2.1.32
(1), we know that
b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}\in\cmonoid_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})\simeq\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Cat})
may now be viewed as a
G
–symmetric monoidal category. We explain now a concrete description of the multiplicative norm functors on
b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}
. First of all, because
\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})
is semiadditive, we get that
\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))
is
G
–semiadditive by
2.4.3
(4). In particular, this means that for any
G
–object
{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}\in\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))
and for any
H\leq G
, we have the counit

\prod_{G/H}\res^{G}_{H}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}\xlongrightarrow{\varepsilon_{{\mathcal{D}}}}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}

from the adjunction
\prod_{G/H}\simeq\coprod_{G/H}\colon\func(BH,\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))\rightleftharpoons\func(BG,\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})):\res^{G}_{H}
. As indicated in the proof of
2.4.3
(4), upon forgetting the
G
–actions, the adjunction counit is given by the multiplication map
\otimes\colon\prod_{|G/H|}{\mathcal{D}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{D}}
. Now note that an object in
\prod_{G/H}\res^{G}_{H}{\mathcal{D}}
admits an explicit description given by a tuple
(X_{g})_{g\in G/H}
and so an object in
(\prod_{G/H}\res^{G}_{H}{\mathcal{D}})^{hG}\simeq{\mathcal{D}}^{hH}
can be described also as the tuple
(gX)_{g\in G/H}
where
X\in{\mathcal{D}}^{hH}
. Since
\varepsilon_{{\mathcal{D}}}
is
G
–equivariant, we then get the map

(\prod_{G/H}\res^{G}_{H}{\mathcal{D}})^{hG}\simeq{\mathcal{D}}^{hH}\xlongrightarrow{\varepsilon_{{\mathcal{D}}}^{hG}}{\mathcal{D}}^{hG}\quad::\quad X\mapsto\bigotimes_{g\in G/H}gX

Now, by virtue of the commuting square of
G
–Bousfield localisations from
2.4.4
, we get from
2.2.6
an identification of
b_{*}\varepsilon_{{\mathcal{D}}}
with the counit in
\underline{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})

\prod_{G/H}\res^{G}_{H}b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}\xlongrightarrow{\varepsilon_{b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}}}b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}

Since this adjunction counit
is
the map encoding the multiplicative norm of an object in
{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})\simeq\mathrm{Cat}_{G}^{\otimes}
, all in all, we see that the
G
–symmetric monoidal category
b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}
has
G/H
–norms given by the formula
X\mapsto\bigotimes_{g\in G/H}gX
.

Because pointwise symmetric monoidal structures are merely cotensors instead of being internal hom objects, the next two lemmas will require a proof separate from, but very much in the spirit of, that of
2.4.3
.

Lemma 2.4.7
.

Let
\underline{J}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
and
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}\in\underline{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})
. Then we have an equivalence
b^{*}\underline{\func}(\underline{J},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\underline{\otimes}})\simeq\func(b^{*}\underline{J},b^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\underline{\otimes}})
in
\func(BG,\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))
.

Proof.

By
[
Sha23
, Prop. 9.7]
, we see that the pairing construction of the pointwise
G
–symmetric monoidal structure from
[
NS22
,
\lx@sectionsign 3.3
]
is compatible with restrictions (for an example argument, see the proof of
[
NS22
, Prop. 3.2.2]
). Hence, we have the left commuting square
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})^{BG}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})^{BG}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\res^{G}_{e}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}(\underline{J},-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(\res^{G}_{e}\underline{J},-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(b^{*}\underline{J},-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\forget}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\forget}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\res^{G}_{e}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\func(\res^{G}_{e}\underline{J},-)}

Furthermore, the category
\func(BG,\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))
is also cotensored over
\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})
under the pointwise symmetric monoidal structure and so we also have the right commuting square in the diagram above.
Now all maps in sight in the left commuting square are moreover
G
–equivariant with the trivial
G
–equivariant structures on all the categories. Hence, the bottom composite of the left square lifts uniquely to the map
b^{*}\underline{\func}(\underline{J},-)\colon{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})\rightarrow\func(BG,\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))
whereas the top composite of the left square lifts uniquely to a map
\func(b^{*}\underline{J},b^{*}-)\colon{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})\rightarrow\func(BG,\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))
(here we have also used the existence of the right commuting square). Hence, all in all, we have obtained an equivalence of functors
b^{*}\underline{\func}(\underline{J},-)\simeq\func(b^{*}\underline{J},b^{*}-)
as required.
∎

Recall our notation of
s\colon\ast\hookrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{G}
being the inclusion of the final object
G/G
from
2.1.10
.

Lemma 2.4.8
.

Let
{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}\in\func(BG,\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))
and
I\in\mathrm{Cat}
. Then there is a natural map
\underline{\func}(s_{!}I,b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\rightarrow b_{*}\func(I,{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})
in
{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})
which is an equivalence.

Proof.

Since
b^{*}s_{!}\simeq\mathrm{triv}_{G}\colon\mathrm{Cat}\rightarrow\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})
and
b^{*}b_{*}\simeq\mathrm{id}
, by
2.4.7
we have an equivalence
b^{*}\underline{\func}(s_{!}I,b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\simeq\func(I,{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})
. Adjointing this over we obtain the claimed map
\underline{\func}(s_{!}I,b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\rightarrow b_{*}\func(I,{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})
in
{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})
. Since the composite
{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}_{G}\xrightarrow{\prod_{H\leq G}(-)^{H}}\prod_{H\leq G}\mathrm{Cat}
is conservative, it is enough to show that the said map is an equivalence upon passing to fixed points for all subgroups of
G
. Without loss of generality, in order to keep notations to a minimum, we may just show it for
G
–fixed points since the other fixed points can be dealt with similarly after restriction. In this case, we need to show that the map in
\mathrm{Cat}

s^{*}\underline{\func}(s_{!}I,b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})\longrightarrow s^{*}b_{*}\func(I,{\mathcal{D}})

is an equivalence. The target is given by
s^{*}b_{*}\func(I,{\mathcal{D}})\simeq\func(I,{\mathcal{D}})^{hG}
, whereas the source is, via
2.1.10
, given by
s^{*}\underline{\func}(s_{!}I,b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})\simeq\func(I,s^{*}b_{*}{\mathcal{D}})\simeq\func(I,{\mathcal{D}}^{hG})
, and it can be checked easily that the map is also the canonical one implementing the limit exchange equivalence
\func(I,{\mathcal{D}}^{hG})\xrightarrow{\simeq}\func(I,{\mathcal{D}})^{hG}
. This concludes the proof of the lemma.
∎

Proposition 2.4.9
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}\in{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})
and
{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}\in\func(BG,\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat}))
. There is a natural equivalence of categories
\func^{\underline{\otimes}}_{G}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\simeq\func^{\otimes}(b^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})^{hG}
.

Proof.

Fix
I\in\mathrm{Cat}
. Consider the following sequence of natural equivalences

\begin{split}\map_{\mathrm{Cat}}\big(I,s^{*}\underline{\func}^{\underline{\otimes}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\big)&\simeq\map_{\mathrm{Cat}_{G}}\big(s_{!}I,\underline{\func}^{\underline{\otimes}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\big)\\
&\simeq\map_{{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})}\big(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},\underline{\func}(s_{!}I,b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\big)\\
&\simeq\map_{{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})}\big(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},b_{*}\func(I,{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\big)\\
&\simeq\map_{\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})^{BG}}\big(b^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},\func(I,{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\big)\\
&\simeq\map_{\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})}\big(b^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},\func(I,{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\big)^{hG}\\
&\simeq\map_{\mathrm{Cat}}\big(I,\func^{\otimes}(b^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})^{hG}\big)\end{split}

where the second and sixth equivalence are by virtue of the universal property from
2.1.33
, the third by
2.4.8
, and the fifth by how the mapping space in
\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})^{BG}
is computed. Since by definition,
s^{*}\underline{\func}^{\underline{\otimes}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})=\func^{\underline{\otimes}}_{G}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},b_{*}{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})
, we obtain the desired equivalence.
∎

We now distil all that we have done in this subsection into the following principle which establishes an abstract but very important link between
G
–categories and their underlying category with
G
–action. We will use the notation
\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}
for the functor
b_{*}\colon\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(\mathrm{Cat})\hookrightarrow\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}
for intuitive appeal. We thank Asaf Horev for discussions leading to it, especially in teaching us the trick of using symmetric monoidal envelopes.

Theorem 2.4.10

(Monoidal Borelification principle)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}\in{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})\simeq\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Cat})
be a
G
–symmetric monoidal category and
{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}\in\func(BG,\cmonoid({\mathrm{Cat}}))
be a symmetric monoidal category with a
G
–action. Then:

1.

The
G
–category
\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}({\mathcal{D}})\in\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
canonically refines to a
G
–symmetric monoidal category
\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}({\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\in{\cmonoid}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})
. The multiplicative norm map
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}\colon{\mathcal{D}}^{hH}\rightarrow{\mathcal{D}}^{hG}
can be concretely described as follows: for
X\in{\mathcal{D}}^{hH}
a
H
–object in
\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}({\mathcal{D}})
, the
G
–object
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}X\in{\mathcal{D}}^{hG}
is given by
\bigotimes_{g\in G/H}gX
,

2.

Writing
{\mathcal{C}}_{e}\in\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})
for the value of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
at
G/e
, the adjunction unit
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}({\mathcal{C}}_{e})
of
2.4.1
canonically refines to a
G
–symmetric monoidal functor
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}({\mathcal{C}}_{e}^{\otimes})
.

3.

There is a natural equivalence
\mathrm{CAlg}_{G}\big(\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}({\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})\big)\simeq\mathrm{CAlg}({\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})^{hG}
.

Proof.

Part (1) is by the fact that the
(b_{*},\forget)
–square in
2.4.4
commutes, and the description of the norm is by
2.4.6
. Part (2) is by the fact that we have a commuting square of
G
–Bousfield localisations from
2.4.4
. And finally, for part (3), we just compute:

\begin{split}\mathrm{CAlg}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}({\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}))&\simeq\func^{\underline{\otimes}}_{G}(\underline{\mathrm{Env}}(\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*}),\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}({\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes}))\\
&\simeq\func^{\otimes}(\mathrm{Env}(\mathrm{Fin}_{*}),{\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})^{hG}\\
&\simeq\mathrm{CAlg}({\mathcal{D}}^{\otimes})^{hG}\end{split}

as required, where the first and last equivalences are by
2.1.32
(2) and the second equivalence is by
2.4.9
.
∎

Remark 2.4.11
.

The structure of
G
–commutative algebra objects and morphisms thereof are often tricky to construct. Part (3) of the theorem guarantees us, however, that at least when the
G
–category involved is Borel, such algebras and their morphisms are nothing but algebras and morphisms in the underlying category equipped with a
G
–action. By further applying suitable
G
–lax symmetric monoidal functors on these Borel
G
–commutative algebras, we may construct out of them many interesting non–Borel examples of
G
–commutative algebras. We refer the reader to
Section

4.4
for an illustration of this strategy.

Remark 2.4.12
.

While we have not pursued it here so as not to obfuscate the general exposition and since we will not be needing it for our purposes, we believe that the notion of Borel objects and its attendant monoidality theory above can be developed more generally for any atomic orbital base category
{\mathcal{T}}
equipped with a full subcategory
b\colon\mathcal{B}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{T}}
which is a
sieve
, i.e. if we are given a morphism
C\rightarrow X
in
{\mathcal{T}}
where
X\in\mathcal{B}
, then
C\in\mathcal{B}
too. The main point is that this will allow the proof of
2.4.1
to go through, from which much else should follow via careful analyses of all the notions involved.

Remark 2.4.13
.

The theorem above is a slight expansion and strengthening of
[
Hil22
, Thm. 3.3.4, Prop. 3.3.6]
from the author’s thesis. Since then, an article
[
Yan23
]
of Lucy Yang’s has appeared that gave a concrete description of
C_{p}
–
\mathbb{E}_{\infty}
–algebras which in particular also yields
2.4.10
(3) in the special of
G=C_{p}
.
