To begin, let us first record some formalities on
{\mathcal{T}}
–semiadditivity.

Lemma 2.5.1
.

Suppose
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–pointed with finite indexed (co)products. Let
f\colon U\rightarrow V
be in
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{/V}
and
Y\in\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. We then have an identification

f_{*}f^{*}\eta_{Y}\simeq\eta_{f_{*}f^{*}Y}\colon f_{*}f^{*}Y\longrightarrow f_{*}f^{*}f_{*}f^{*}Y

Proof.

This is an immediate consequence of
2.2.6
, using the adjointable square
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}}

coming from the fact that both the restriction functor
f^{*}\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow f_{*}f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
and indexed product functor
f_{*}\colon f_{*}f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
preserve indexed products.
∎

Observation 2.5.2
.

Suppose
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–pointed with finite indexed products. Let
f\colon U\rightarrow V
be in
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{/V}
and let
X\in f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. Observe that
X
is a retract of
f^{*}f_{*}X
since, by the pullback decomposition from
Eq.

5
, we have
f^{*}f_{*}X\simeq X\times\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}X
. Hence, using the map
\ast\rightarrow\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}X\rightarrow\ast
, we can get a retraction

X\simeq X\times\ast\longrightarrow f^{*}f_{*}X\simeq X\times\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}X\xlongrightarrow{\pi}X\simeq X\times\ast

Corollary 2.5.3
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–pointed category admitting finite indexed products. Let
f\colon U\rightarrow V
be in
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{/V}
and let
X\in f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. Then the composite

f_{*}X\xlongrightarrow{\eta_{f_{*}X}}f_{*}f^{*}f_{*}X\xlongrightarrow{f_{*}\pi}f_{*}X

is an equivalence.

Proof.

Since retractions of equivalences are equivalences, by
2.5.2
which gives that
X
is a retract of
f^{*}f_{*}X
, it suffices to show the equivalence when
X=f^{*}Y
for some
Y\in\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. But then, in this case, this composite is identified with

f_{*}f^{*}Y\xlongrightarrow{f_{*}f^{*}\eta_{Y}}f_{*}f^{*}f_{*}f^{*}Y\xlongrightarrow{f_{*}\pi}f_{*}f^{*}Y

(12)

by
2.5.1
. Now by a simple unwinding of adjunctions, we see via the decomposition from
Eq.

5
that
f^{*}\eta_{Y}\colon f^{*}Y\rightarrow f^{*}f_{*}f^{*}Y\simeq f^{*}Y\times\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}f^{*}Y
has the effect of the identity map on the
f^{*}Y
component in
f^{*}f_{*}f^{*}Y
. Therefore, we see indeed that the composite
Eq.

12
is indeed an equivalence.
∎

Proof.

We only show that
\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{{\mathcal{T}},L,\kappa}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–semiadditive. This would then imply that the
{\mathcal{T}}
–full subcategory
\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{{\mathcal{T}},\mathrm{st},L,\kappa}
is too, since
{\mathcal{T}}
–presentable-stables are closed under
{\mathcal{T}}
–products.

First, we show that
\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{{\mathcal{T}},L,\kappa}
is ordinary semiadditive. Recall from
2.1.34
that we may view
\mathrm{Pr}_{{\mathcal{T}},L,\kappa}
as a non–full subcategory of
\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Pr}_{L,\kappa})
consisting of those objects for which all the restriction functors have left adjoints and satisfy the left Beck–Chevalley condition, and the morphisms are those which satsify the left Beck–Chevalley condition. Since we already know that
\mathrm{Pr}_{L,\kappa}
is semiadditive (cf. for instance
[
HL13
, Ex. 4.3.11]
), it suffices now to argue that
\mathrm{Pr}_{{\mathcal{T}},L,\kappa}\subset\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Pr}_{L,\kappa})
creates finite (co)products by applying
2.2.11
. Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}\in\mathrm{Pr}_{{\mathcal{T}},L,\kappa}
. The product and coproduct
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{1}\times\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}
clearly still satisfies Beck–Chevalley, and the projection maps
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{1}\times\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}
and inclusion maps
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{1}\times\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}
(defined using that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}
had initial objects) also clearly satisfies Beck–Chevalley. These give condition (1), and to see condition (2), suppose we are given
h_{i}\colon\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}
and
f_{i}\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{E}}

all satisfying Beck–Chevalley. Then it is similarly easy to see that the maps
h_{1}\times h_{2}\colon\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{1}\times\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}
and
f_{1}\sqcup f_{2}\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{1}\times\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{E}}
also satisfy Beck–Chevalley, whence condition (2) as wanted.

Next, we show that there is a canonical adjunction datum witnessing that
f_{*}\dashv f^{*}
for every
f\colon W\rightarrow V
in
\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. For this, simply observe the natural equivalences

where the first and last equivalences is by
2.2.15
, and the middle equivalence is by
[
Hil22a
, Prop. 6.6.2]
. Now write
\eta,\varepsilon
as the adjunction (co)unit for
f^{*}\dashv f_{*}
in
\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{R,\kappa\text{-filt}}
and
\widetilde{\eta},\widetilde{\varepsilon}
for the
f_{*}\dashv f^{*}
(co)unit in
\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{L,\kappa}
. Tracing through the identifications above, we obtain that
\widetilde{\eta}\dashv\varepsilon
and
\widetilde{{\varepsilon}}\dashv\eta
. Under these notations, the Beck–Chevalley equivalences
f^{*}f_{*}\simeq\mathrm{id}\sqcup\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}
and
f^{*}f_{*}\simeq\mathrm{id}\times\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}
are then implemented by

\widetilde{\mathrm{BC}}\colon\mathrm{id}\sqcup\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}\xlongrightarrow{(\mathrm{id}\sqcup\overline{c}_{*}c^{*})\widetilde{\eta}^{f}}(\mathrm{id}\sqcup\overline{c}_{*}c^{*})f^{*}f_{*}\simeq(\mathrm{id}\sqcup\overline{c}_{*}\overline{c}^{*})f^{*}f_{*}\xlongrightarrow{\widetilde{\varepsilon}^{\overline{c}}_{f^{*}f_{*}}}f^{*}f_{*}

\mathrm{BC}\colon f^{*}f_{*}\xlongrightarrow{\eta^{\overline{c}}_{f^{*}f_{*}}}(\mathrm{id}\times\overline{c}_{*}\overline{c}^{*})f^{*}f_{*}\simeq(\mathrm{id}\times\overline{c}_{*}{c}^{*})f^{*}f_{*}\xlongrightarrow{(\mathrm{id}\times\overline{c}_{*}c^{*})\varepsilon^{f}}\mathrm{id}\times\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}

Now since
\widetilde{\mathrm{BC}}
was an equivalence, an inverse is given by the right adjoint, which may in turn be seen easily to be given by
\mathrm{BC}
. Therefore, the composite
\mathrm{BC}\circ\widetilde{\mathrm{BC}}\colon\mathrm{id}\sqcup\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}\rightarrow\mathrm{id}\times\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}

is
the semiadditive equivalence
\sqcup\simeq\times
. In particular, we have the equivalence of maps

(\mathrm{id}\sqcup\emptyset)\simeq(\mathrm{id}\times\emptyset)\circ\mathrm{BC}\circ\widetilde{\mathrm{BC}}\colon\mathrm{id}\sqcup\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}\longrightarrow\mathrm{id}

(13)

Finally, to see that
\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{{\mathcal{T}},L,\kappa}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–semiadditive via
f_{*}\dashv f^{*}
, we need to show that the composite

is closed under finite indexed products. Hence, since arbitrary parametrised limits can be decomposed into arbitrary fibrewise limit and finite indexed products, we are left to argue in the case of arbitrary fibrewise limits. This can in turn be split up into showing the case of arbitrary products and pullbacks. We will only treat the case of pullbacks since that of arbitrary products is simpler.

We would like to apply
2.2.11
. Since fibrewise limits in
{\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}}=\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}})
are computed pointwise and since we already know from the unparametrised case that

are closed under limits, we know that

–pullbacks
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{1}\times_{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{3}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}

2.2.7

\mathrm{Pr}_{{\mathcal{T}},R,\mathrm{st},\kappa\text{-filt}}
. Moreover, the projection maps
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{1}\times_{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{3}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}

2.2.11

\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{1}\times_{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{3}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}

{\mathcal{T}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{a}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{!}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}}

whence the

{\mathcal{T}}
–exact. Since arbitrary limits can be decomposed in terms of arbitrary products and pullbacks and the case of products is simple to see, we will only argue in the case of pullbacks. In this case, we need to argue that the projection maps
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{1}\times_{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{3}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}
preserve finite indexed products for
i\in\{1,2,3\}
. But this is clear since
{\mathcal{T}}
–biproducts in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{1}\times_{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{3}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}
are created pointwise.
∎

]

to0.0pt{\hss\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.0pt\raisebox{0.5pt}[0.0pt]{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{Sp}$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip to0.0pt{\hskip-0.19133pt\raisebox{0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{Sp}$}\hss}\mbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{Sp}$}}}}^{\underline{\omega}})
are
\omega
–compact objects. To see that the two functors of
Eq.

14
are jointly conservative, suppose
\varphi:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is a functor such that

\varphi:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{{\simeq}}\xrightarrow{\simeq}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{{\simeq}}\quad\quad\text{ and }\quad\quad\varphi:\underline{\func}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\simeq}\xrightarrow{\simeq}\underline{\func}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})^{{\simeq}}

are equivalences of
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–spaces. In particular, the first equivalence implies that
\varphi
is
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–essentially surjective. On the other hand, the fibre over
[W\rightarrow V]
of
\underline{\func}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is
\func(\Delta^{1},{\mathcal{C}}_{W})
and so the second equivalence together with the the formula for unparametrised mapping spaces as pullbacks
\func(\Delta^{1},{\mathcal{C}}_{W})\times_{{\mathcal{C}}_{W}^{\times 2}}\{\ast\}
gives us that
\varphi:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–fully faithful. Therefore,
\varphi
is an equivalence, as wanted, and so by
2.2.14
, we may conclude the proof.
∎

, Cor. 6.7.1]

is conservative and preserves (co)limits. On the other hand, the diagonal functor in

preserves arbitrary (co)limits by
2.5.10
. Combining these, we get that the vertical functor in
Eq.

16
preserves arbitrary (co)limits in addition to being conservative from the previous paragraph, and hence by
2.2.12
it also reflects (co)limits, as wanted.
∎

For the purposes of our motivic analyses later, we will also record here the following:

Proposition 2.5.13
.

Fix
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Pr}_{{\mathcal{T}},L,\kappa}
. The functor
\underline{\func}(-,\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\colon\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{{\mathcal{T}},L,\kappa}
taken along left Kan extensions preserve finite parametrised colimits.

Proof.

Since every finite parametrised colimit can be decomposed as the finite indexed coproducts and finite fibrewise colimits, we will split up the proof into these two cases. For the indexed coproducts, we just note that for a fixed
f\colon U\rightarrow V
in
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{/V}
, we have
\underline{\func}(f_{!}\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\simeq f_{*}f^{*}\underline{\func}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
, and so since
2.5.4
gives that
f_{*}f^{*}\underline{\func}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is also the indexed coproduct in
\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{{\mathcal{T}},L,\kappa}
, we are done in this case. Since we have argued for an arbitrary
U\in\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
, this also covers the case of ordinary finite coproducts by setting
U=\coprod_{i=1}^{n}V
.

Hence, we are left with showing the case of pushouts. Suppose we have a pushout diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{I}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{J}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{K}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{P}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}

By
2.5.5
, we have an equivalence
\underline{\func}(\underline{P},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\simeq\underline{\func}(\underline{J},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\times_{\underline{\func}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}\underline{\func}(\underline{K},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
in
\underline{\mathrm{Pr}}_{{\mathcal{T}},R,\kappa\text{-filt}}
using the restriction maps

, and so upon passing to left adjoints under

3
The theory of parametrised cubes

In this section, we lay down the theory of parametrised cubes associated to atomic orbital base categories
{\mathcal{T}}
. As we shall see in
3.1.5
, this hypothesis on
{\mathcal{T}}
will be exploited in an essential way to identify the “singletons” in a parametrised cube, which will in turn play a key role in our treatment of
C_{2}
–pushouts in the setting of equivariant K–theory in
Section

4.3
. The key insight is that the inclusions of the initial and final objects in
\Delta^{1}
will allow us to encode the idea of a “subset” in a purely abstract and categorical manner (where
1
means being in a “subset” and
0
means the converse). The advantage of this point of view is at least two–fold in that it not only lets one speak of cubes in a very general setting but also allows many proofs to be carried out using concise adjunction manipulations.

As far as we are aware, this use case of atomic orbitality of base categories is new and might represent a third expression – alongside that of
{\mathcal{T}}
–semiadditivity and
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidality for which it was first designed by
[
BDG+16
]
– of the algebraic richness of the atomic orbitality hypothesis. As alluded to in the introduction, the rather general and abstract treatment of cubes here will serve as the foundations for a theory of parametrised functor calculus, a subject that will be treated in forthcoming work.

We now outline the contents of this section: in
Section

3.1
, we will introduce the basic definitions and constructions of cubes; we will then provide a general utility (co)limit decomposition result
3.2.2
and record the interaction of parametrised tensor powers with cofibres as
3.2.8
in
Section

3.2
; lastly, we will specialise the general theory to the equivariant setting where we look at
G/H
–cubes when
|G/H|=2
in preparation for our K–theoretic applications in
Section

4.3
.

3.1
Basic notions

Definition 3.1.1
.

Let
w\colon W\rightarrow T
be a map in
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
and let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category. We write
\underline{\Delta}^{1}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{T}=\func({\mathcal{T}}_{/T}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
for the constant
{\mathcal{T}}_{/T}
–category with value
\Delta^{1}
. By
the parametrised
w
–cube
we will mean the
{\mathcal{T}}_{/T}
–category
w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
and by
a parametrised
w
–cube in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
we will mean a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor
Q\colon w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
.

Proposition 3.1.2
.

The parametrised cubes
w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
are all parametrised posets, i.e. they belong to the full subcategory
\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Poset})\subseteq\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
. In fact, these are fibrewise given by cubes of various dimensions.

Proof.

This is just because the inclusion
\mathrm{Poset}\subseteq\mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}
preserves all limits (with left adjoint
\tau_{\leq-1}
) and hence in particular preserves products. On the other hand, we know that for any
{\mathcal{C}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}
admitting finite products,
\cofree({\mathcal{C}})
also have all indexed products coming from the products on
{\mathcal{C}}
. Therefore all in all,
\cofree(\mathrm{Poset})\subseteq\cofree(\mathrm{Cat}_{\infty})
admits (and is closed under) indexed products. In particular, since
\underline{\Delta}^{1}
is a parametrised poset, so is
w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
as required. The last statement is simply because these indexed products are computed as various products in
\mathrm{Poset}
of
\Delta^{1}
, which are cubes.
∎

Construction 3.1.3
.

Upon applying
\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},-)
, the join–slice adjunction (cf. for instance
[
Lan21
, Cor. 1.4.17]
) induces the parametrised join–slice adjunction

(-)^{\underline{\triangleleft}}\colon\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}},\underline{\ast}/}:(-)_{p/}

where
(-)_{p/}
is the slice construction on a category equipped with a choice of object, i.e.
(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},d)_{/p}\coloneqq\underline{\ast}\times_{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\Delta^{1}}
where the map
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{{\Delta}^{1}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is the source map. In particular, if
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
has an initial object
\ast
, then any functor
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
will induce an extension
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\triangleleft}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
.

We thank Sil Linskens for pointing out the need for the strict initial object assumption in the following result.

Proposition 3.1.4
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category with a strict initial object (i.e. any morphism to the initial object in
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
must be an equivalence) and
F\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
be an arbitrary fully faithful
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor whose essential image does not contain the initial object of
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
. Then the extension
F^{\underline{\triangleleft}}\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\triangleleft}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is also fully faithful.

Proof.

Since fully faithfulness is a fibrewise notion, we can just prove this fibrewise and hence reduce to proving it in the unparametrised case. Since we already know that the composite
{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}^{\triangleleft}\rightarrow{\mathcal{D}}
is fully faithful and since, on the space of objects, it is standard that
({\mathcal{C}}^{\triangleleft})^{\simeq}\simeq{\mathcal{C}}^{\simeq}\sqcup\{\emptyset_{{\mathcal{C}}}\}
(see for example
[
CMN+20
, Prop. A.4]
), we are left to argue that the induced map of mapping spaces is an equivalence when one of the objects is
\emptyset_{{\mathcal{C}}}
the initial object in
{\mathcal{C}}^{\triangleleft}
. To this end, first note that
\emptyset_{{\mathcal{C}}}
does not admit any map from any
X\in{\mathcal{C}}
: this is because we have a functor
{\mathcal{C}}^{\triangleleft}\rightarrow\ast^{\triangleleft}\simeq\Delta^{1}
, and so any such map would give a map from 1 to 0 in
\Delta^{1}
, which does not exist. Thus the object
\emptyset_{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\triangleleft}}
is also a strict initial object. Hence, we are left to argue that
\map_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\triangleleft}}(\emptyset_{{\mathcal{C}}},X)\rightarrow\map_{{\mathcal{D}}}(F^{\triangleleft}(\emptyset_{{\mathcal{C}}}),F^{\triangleleft}(X))
is an equivalence. But this is true because by the universal property, we must have that
F^{\triangleleft}(\emptyset_{{\mathcal{C}}})\simeq\emptyset_{{\mathcal{D}}}
, and so both sides are contractible.
∎

The following is the key construction in the theory of parametrised cubes.

Construction 3.1.5

(Singleton inclusion)
.

Let
w\colon W\rightarrow T
be a map in
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. We would like to construct a map

\psi_{w}\colon w_{!}w^{*}\underline{\ast}\longrightarrow w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}

which generalises the inclusion of the singletons in Goodwillie’s definition of strong cocartesianness. First note by atomic orbitality that we have the pullback in
\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W\coprod C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\coprod c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\coprod\overline{c}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}

(17)

where
C
is some object in
\mathrm{Fin}_{\mathcal{T}}
. In particular, we have the decomposition

w^{*}w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\simeq\mathrm{id}_{*}\mathrm{id}^{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\times\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\simeq w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\times\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}

Now by adjunction, to construct
\psi_{w}
, it would suffice to construct its adjoint
\overline{\psi}_{w}\colon w^{*}\underline{\ast}\rightarrow w^{*}w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
. By the decomposition above, this is equivalent to constructing maps

w^{*}\underline{\ast}\rightarrow w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\quad\quad\quad\big(w^{*}\underline{\ast}\rightarrow\overline{{c}}_{*}c^{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\big)\Leftrightarrow\big(\overline{c}^{*}w^{*}\underline{\ast}\simeq c^{*}w^{*}\underline{\ast}\rightarrow c^{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\big)

To this end, we declare the first map to be the inclusion of the target and the second map to be the inclusion of the source. This yields the map
\psi_{w}
which one should think of the inclusion of the singletons in a cube. We will see that this is always fully faithful in
3.1.8
.
Therefore, by
3.1.3
, the map
\psi_{w}
constructed above induces a map

\varphi_{w}\colon(w_{!}w^{*}\underline{\ast})^{\underline{\triangleleft}}\longrightarrow w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}

This map
\varphi_{w}
should be thought of generalising the subsets of size at most 1 in a cube, as the following important example will illustrate.

Example 3.1.6
.

In the special case when
T\in{\mathcal{T}}
is the final object,
W=\coprod^{n}_{j=1}T
, and
w\colon W\rightarrow T
is the fold map, we will see how the above construction yields the usual inclusion of singletons in the
n
–cube
\prod^{n}_{j=1}\Delta^{1}=\poset([n])
. To wit, since
T\times T\simeq T
by finality, we have a decomposition

(\coprod^{n}_{j=1}T)\times(\coprod^{n}_{j=1}T)\simeq\coprod_{\begin{subarray}{c}(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}/n\times\mathbb{Z}/n,\\
a-b\equiv_{n}0\end{subarray}}T\sqcup\coprod_{j=1}^{n-1}\coprod_{\begin{subarray}{c}(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}/n\times\mathbb{Z}/n,\\
a-b\equiv_{n}j\end{subarray}}T

where the term
\coprod_{\begin{subarray}{c}(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}/n\times\mathbb{Z}/n,\\
a-b\equiv_{n}0\end{subarray}}T
should be thought of as the diagonal tuples in
(\coprod^{n}T)\times(\coprod^{n}T)
.
Hence, the pullback
Eq.

17
in this case looks like
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\displaystyle{\coprod_{\begin{subarray}{c}(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}/n\times\mathbb{Z}/n,\\
a-b\equiv_{n}0\end{subarray}}T\sqcup\coprod_{j=1}^{n-1}\coprod_{\begin{subarray}{c}(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}/n\times\mathbb{Z}/n,\\
a-b\equiv_{n}j\end{subarray}}T}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod^{n}_{j=1}T}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod^{n}_{j=1}T}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\sqcup c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\sqcup\overline{c}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}

In this case, the map
\psi\colon\coprod_{j=1}^{n}\underline{\ast}\simeq w_{!}\underline{\ast}\rightarrow\prod_{j=1}^{n}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\simeq w_{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
constructed in
3.1.5
comes from specifying the map
w^{*}\underline{\ast}\rightarrow w^{*}w_{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\simeq\underline{\Delta}^{1}\times\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
describable as

(\ast,\ldots,\ast)\longrightarrow(\Delta^{1}\times\prod_{1\leq j\leq n,j\neq 1}\Delta^{1},\Delta^{1}\times\prod_{1\leq j\leq n,j\neq 2}\Delta^{1},\ldots,\Delta^{1}\times\prod_{1\leq j\leq n,j\neq n}\Delta^{1})

choosing
1
in the first copy of
\Delta^{1}
and
0
’s in
\prod_{1\leq j\leq n,j\neq k}\Delta^{1}
for all
k
. Equivalently, the
k
–th summand in
w_{!}\underline{\ast}\simeq\coprod_{j=1}^{n}\ast
picks out
1
in the
k
–th copy of
\Delta^{1}
in
\prod_{1\leq j\leq n}\Delta^{1}
and
0
’s in the other copies of
\Delta^{1}
. Hence, the
k
–th summand in
w_{!}\underline{\ast}
sits as the
k
–th singleton in
\prod_{j=1}^{n}\Delta^{1}\simeq\poset([n])
, as claimed.

We now record the following fundamental observation which will serve both as a basic principle for our proofs as well as as an indication that our notion of singletons is “correct” from the parametrised point of view, in that it is a notion that is stable under basechange along arbitrary morphisms in
{\mathcal{T}}
.

Remark 3.1.7

(Stability of singleton inclusions under basechange)
.

Let
b\colon B\rightarrow T
be a map in
{\mathcal{T}}
. Recall first that we have an adjunction from
2.1.20

b_{!}\colon\mathrm{Fin}_{B}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Fin}_{T}:b^{*}

where
b_{!}
is given by postcomposing with
b\colon B\rightarrow T
and
b^{*}
is pullback along
b
. In particular, applying
b^{*}
to the pullback
Eq.

17
gives us a pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}W\coprod b^{*}C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\coprod{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\coprod\overline{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{w}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{w}}

We would like to show now that
b^{*}\psi_{w}\simeq\psi_{\overline{w}}
, so that singleton inclusions are stable under basechange.

By pasting pullback squares, we also see that we have the pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}

(18)

Now recall that the adjoint of
\psi_{w}
was a map defined as the composite

w^{*}\underline{\ast}\hookrightarrow w^{*}\underline{\ast}\amalg\overline{c}_{!}c^{*}w^{*}\underline{\ast}\xlongrightarrow{w^{*}\psi_{w}\simeq\big((1,0)\>(0,0)\big)}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\times\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}

Here, the map
\big((1,0)\>(0,0)\big)
is matrix notation for the map induced by the four maps

w^{*}\underline{\ast}\xrightarrow{1}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\quad\quad w^{*}\underline{\ast}\xrightarrow{0}\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\quad\quad\overline{c}_{!}c^{*}w^{*}\underline{\ast}\xrightarrow{0}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\quad\quad\overline{c}_{!}c^{*}w^{*}\underline{\ast}\xrightarrow{0}\overline{c}_{*}c^{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}

We claim now that
b^{*}\psi_{w}\colon\overline{w}_{!}\overline{w}\underline{\ast}\rightarrow\overline{w}_{*}\overline{w}^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
is defined similarly, so that
b^{*}\psi_{w}\simeq\psi_{\overline{w}}
as wanted. Adjoining over
b^{*}\psi_{w}
gives the map

\overline{w}^{*}\underline{\ast}\hookrightarrow\overline{w}^{*}\underline{\ast}\amalg\overline{a}_{!}a^{*}\underline{\ast}\xlongrightarrow{\overline{w}^{*}b^{*}\psi_{w}}\overline{w}^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\times\overline{a}_{*}a^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}

(19)

But then
\overline{w}^{*}b^{*}\simeq z^{*}w^{*}
, and so together with the pullback
Eq.

18
, the map
\overline{w}^{*}b^{*}\psi_{w}
from
Eq.

19
can be analysed as

z^{*}w^{*}\underline{\ast}\amalg\overline{a}_{!}a^{*}\underline{\ast}\xlongrightarrow{z^{*}w^{*}\psi_{w}\simeq((1,0)\>(0,0))}z^{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\times\overline{a}_{*}a^{*}\overline{w}^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}

which is the desired form of map.

Corollary 3.1.8
.

The map
\varphi_{w}\colon(w_{!}w^{*}\underline{\ast})^{\underline{\triangleleft}}\rightarrow w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
is fully faithful.

Proof.

By
3.1.4
, it suffices to show that the map
\psi_{w}\colon w_{!}w^{*}\underline{\ast}\rightarrow w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
is fully faithful. Now, since fully faithfulness is a fibrewise notion, it suffices to check the statement in each fibre, and since these maps are stable under basechange by
3.1.7
, we may without loss of generality argue in the fibre over
T\in{\mathcal{T}}
. In case
w\colon W\rightarrow T
is not an equivalence, then we know by
2.1.18
that
\mathrm{ev}_{T}(w_{!}\underline{\ast})\simeq\emptyset
, and so the map
\psi_{w}
is vacuously fully faithful in the fibre over
T\in{\mathcal{T}}
. On the other hand, if
w\colon W\rightarrow T
were an equivalence, then the map
\psi_{w}\colon w_{!}\underline{\ast}\rightarrow w_{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
is just the inclusion of
0
in
\Delta^{1}
, which is also fully faithful. Hence,
\psi
is fully faithful in either case, as was to be shown.
∎

Example 3.1.9

(
G
–cubes and
C_{2}
–pushouts)
.

Let
G
be a finite group,
H\leq G
a subgroup, and consider the case of
{\mathcal{T}}=\mathcal{O}_{G}
. The
G
–category
w_{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}=\prod_{G/H}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
should then be thought of as the
|G/H|
–dimensional cube equipped with the
G
–action dictated by the one on
G/H
. For example, one would expect such a diagram to have
G
–fixed points only the initial and the final object, and the underlying diagram to be a
|G/H|
–cube. And indeed, we do have that
\mathrm{ev}_{G/G}(w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1})\simeq\Delta^{1}
and
\mathrm{ev}_{G/e}(w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1})\simeq\prod_{|G/H|}\Delta^{1}
, as expected. In the rest of the article, we will be especially interested in the case when
|G/H|=2
. In this case, a
G
–diagram indexed by
(w_{!}w^{*}\underline{\ast})^{\underline{\triangleleft}}\subseteq w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
may be schematically represented as the datum
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

where
A
is a
G
–object,
B
is a
H
–object, the maps
f
are maps of
H
–objects
\res^{G}_{H}A\xrightarrow{f}B
, and the
G
–action on
G/H
swaps the two copies of
f
’s. We will call the
G
–colimits of such diagrams
C_{2}
–pushouts
for reasons that we hope are clear given this schematic representation. In the next section, we will give a formula to compute such
G
–colimits in terms of ordinary pushouts and indexed coproducts.

3.2
Cubical decompositions

We would like now to apply the general nonsense
2.2.10
to the cubical setting, the highlights of which are the decomposition
3.2.2
and
3.2.8
.

Observation 3.2.1
.

Let
\underline{I}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. Then there is a pushout in
\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}=\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{I}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\ast}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{I}\times\underline{\Delta}^{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleright}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi}

To see this, since all constructions and operations in sight in the square above are done fibrewise, we may reduce to showing the statement in the unparametrised case in
\mathrm{Cat}
. Here, we know that we have the join–slice adjunction (cf. for instance
[
Lan21
, Cor. 1.4.17]
)

(-)^{\triangleright}\colon\mathrm{Cat}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Cat}_{\ast/}:(-)_{/p}

where
(-)_{/p}
is the slice construction on a category equipped with a choice of object, i.e.
({\mathcal{D}},d)_{/p}\coloneqq\ast\times_{{\mathcal{D}}}{\mathcal{D}}^{\Delta^{1}}
where
{\mathcal{D}}^{\Delta^{1}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{D}}
is the target projection. Hence, we just need to show that the pushout construction
P(I)\coloneqq(I\times\Delta^{1})\cup_{I}\ast
is also left adjoint to
(-){/p}
. For this, let
({\mathcal{D}},d)\in\mathrm{Cat}_{\ast/}
and simply consider

\begin{split}\map_{\mathrm{Cat}_{\ast/}}(P(I),({\mathcal{D}},d))&\simeq\map_{\mathrm{Cat}}(P(I),{\mathcal{D}})\times_{\map_{\mathrm{Cat}}(\ast,{\mathcal{D}})}\{d\}\\
&\simeq\map_{\mathrm{Cat}}(I\times\Delta^{1},{\mathcal{D}})\times_{\map_{\mathrm{Cat}}(I,{\mathcal{D}})}\{d\}\\
&\simeq\map_{\mathrm{Cat}}(I,{\mathcal{D}}^{\Delta^{1}}\times_{{\mathcal{D}}}\ast)=\map_{\mathrm{Cat}}(I,({\mathcal{D}},d)_{/p})\end{split}

as required.

Using the notations from the pushout in the observation above, we may now extract the following important decomposition result for parametrised (co)limits that we will be especially interested in.

Proposition 3.2.2
.

Let
i\colon\underline{I}\hookrightarrow\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleright}}
be the inclusion and let the morphism
\mathrm{can}\colon i^{*}\rightarrow c^{*}\ell^{*}
in
\underline{\func}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
be the canonical structure map. The limit functor
\underline{\lim}_{\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleright}}}\colon\underline{\func}(\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleright}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
can be computed as follows: letting
\partial\in\underline{\func}(\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleright}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
, we have a pullback in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\lim}_{\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleright}}}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell^{*}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c_{*}i^{*}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c_{*}c^{*}\ell^{*}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c_{*}\mathrm{can}}

Similarly, for any
\partial\in\underline{\func}(\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleleft}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
, we obtain the pushout decomposition
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c_{!}c^{*}\ell^{*}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell^{*}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c_{!}i^{*}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleleft}}}\partial}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c_{!}\mathrm{can}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}

Proof.

We will first need to collect a few elementary formal observations:

•

Since the inclusion of the source
s\colon\underline{I}\hookrightarrow\underline{I}\times\underline{\Delta}^{1}
has a right adjoint
f
(because
0\in\Delta^{1}
is an initial object), we get that
f^{*}\dashv s^{*}
and so
s^{*}\simeq f_{*}
.

•

Hence, if we write
v\colon\underline{I}\times\underline{\Delta}^{1}\rightarrow\underline{\ast}
for the unique map, then since
v\simeq cf
, we get
v_{*}\simeq c_{*}f_{*}\simeq c_{*}s^{*}
.

•

Moreover, since
ft\simeq\mathrm{id}
, we also get that
s^{*}t_{*}\simeq f_{*}t_{*}\simeq\mathrm{id}
.

•

Next, since
\pi s\simeq i
, we get
s^{*}\pi^{*}\simeq i^{*}
.

•

Under these identifications, the canonical map in the statement of the result can be obtained by applying
s^{*}
to
\eta^{t}_{\pi^{*}}\colon\pi^{*}\rightarrow t_{*}t^{*}\pi^{*}
since
s^{*}\pi^{*}\simeq i^{*}
and
s^{*}t_{*}t^{*}\pi^{*}\simeq\mathrm{id}\circ c^{*}\ell^{*}\simeq c^{*}\ell^{*}
. It is a straightforward check to see that this is the canonical structure map.

Now, by
3.2.1
, we have a pullback description of
\underline{\func}(\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleright}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
as

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}(\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleright}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\Delta}^{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi^{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t^{*}}

(20)

Hence, by
2.2.9
, we then get the pullback diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\lim}_{\underline{I}^{\underline{\triangleright}}}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell^{*}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v_{*}\pi^{*}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c_{*}t^{*}\pi^{*}\partial\simeq c_{*}c^{*}\ell^{*}\partial}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta^{c}_{\ell^{*}\partial}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v_{*}\eta^{t}_{\pi^{*}\partial}}

The identifications above now allow us to conclude that this pullback is of the form in the statement of the result. As usual, the the case of colimits can now be deduced be deduced by passing to opposite categories.
∎

Construction 3.2.3
.

We view the inclusion
\Lambda^{2}_{0}\subseteq(\Delta^{1})^{\times 2}
as
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 00}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 10}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 00}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 10}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 01}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 01}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 11}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hookrightarrow}

In this way, for any
n\geq 1
, we may describe the objects in the full subcategory
\prod^{n}_{i=1}\Lambda^{2}_{0}\subseteq\prod^{n}_{i=1}(\Delta^{1})^{\times 2}
as those tuples
(a_{i})_{1\leq i\leq n}
where
a_{i}\in\{00,10,01\}
. We want to decompose
\prod^{n}_{i=1}\Lambda^{2}_{0}
in terms of subcategories that we will now specify:

•

Let
M_{n}\subseteq\prod^{n}_{i=1}\Lambda^{2}_{0}
be the full subcategory
(\prod^{n}_{i=1}\Delta^{1})\times\{0\}
. Concretely in terms of the tuples description above, this is the full subcategory consisting of those tuples such that
a_{i}\in\{00,10\}
.

•

Let
B_{n}\subseteq\prod^{n}_{i=1}\Lambda^{2}_{0}
be the full subcategory
\prod^{n}_{i=1}\Lambda^{2}_{0}\backslash\{(10,\ldots,10)\}
, i.e. of those tuples where some of the
a_{i}
’s must either be
00
or
01
.

•

Let
F_{n}\subseteq B_{n}
be the full subcategory of those tuples where
a_{i}\in\{01,10\}
, that is, where none of the
a_{i}
’s are
00
and at least one of them is
01
.

•

Let
J_{n}\coloneqq T_{n}\cap B_{n}
.

Similarly, since for any map
f\colon U\rightarrow V
in
{\mathcal{T}}
,
f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0}
is fibrewise just products of multiple copies of
\Lambda^{2}_{0}
, we may similarly define in a fibrewise fashion the
{\mathcal{T}}
–full subcategories
\underline{J}_{f},\underline{F}_{f},\underline{B}_{f},\underline{M}_{f}\subseteq f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0}
. Here,
\underline{J}_{f},\underline{B}_{f},\underline{M}_{f}
are clearly
{\mathcal{T}}
–subcategories, and to see that
\underline{F}_{f}
is too, we need to argue that it is closed under restrictions. More precisely, we need to show that if
A\xrightarrow{a}W\xrightarrow{w}V
are maps in
{\mathcal{T}}
, then the map
(\underline{F}_{f})_{W}\subseteq(f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0})_{W}\xrightarrow{a^{*}}(f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0})_{A}
factors through
(\underline{F}_{f})_{A}
. For this, let us set up some notations and consider the pullback diagram in
\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{i,j}Y_{ij}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{i}Z_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sqcup p_{ij}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sqcup q_{ij}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sqcup u_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sqcup v_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}

We then get
(f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0})_{W}\simeq(w^{*}f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0})_{W}\simeq(\prod_{i}u_{i*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0})_{W}\simeq\prod_{i}\Lambda^{2}_{0}
and
(a^{*}w^{*}f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0})_{A}\simeq(\prod_{i}\prod_{j}p_{ij*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0})_{A}\simeq\prod_{i}\prod_{j}\Lambda^{2}_{0}
. Under these identifications, the map
(f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0})_{W}\xrightarrow{a^{*}}(f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0})_{A}
is then simply the product
\prod_{i}\Delta\colon\prod_{i}\Lambda^{2}_{0}\rightarrow\prod_{i}\prod_{j}\Lambda^{2}_{0}
of the diagonal maps. From the tuples definition of
F_{n}
above, it is then clear that
(\underline{F}_{f})_{W}\subseteq\prod_{i}\Lambda^{2}_{0}
is sent to
(\underline{F}_{f})_{A}\subseteq\prod_{i}\prod_{j}\Lambda^{2}_{0}
as was to be argued.

Observation 3.2.4
.

The reason we will be interested in the subcategories above is that we have a union of posets
\prod^{n}_{i=1}\Lambda^{2}_{0}=M_{n}\cup_{J_{n}}B_{n}
and so we have a pushout in
\mathrm{Cat}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces J_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{i=1}^{n}\Lambda^{2}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}

One way to see this is that fully faithful inclusions of posets induce monomorphisms of their associated simplicial sets under the nerve functor, and so such inclusions are in particular cofibrations in the Joyal model structure (cf.
[
Lur09
, Thm. 2.2.5.1]
), whence the strict pushout being a homotopy pushout in
\mathrm{Cat}
.
Hence, since pushouts in
\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}=\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
are computed pointwise, we also have a pushout in
\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{J}_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{M}_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{B}_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}

Lemma 3.2.5
.

The inclusion
F_{n}\subseteq B_{n}
is cofinal.

Proof.

To apply Quillen’s Theorem A (e.g.
[
Lan21
, Thm. 4.4.20]
), we need to show that for every tuple
\underline{a}\in B_{n}
, the category
(F_{n})_{\underline{a}/}
is weakly contractible. We will show this by showing that
(F_{n})_{\underline{a}/}
has an initial object.
To this end, consider the tuple
\widetilde{\underline{a}}
defined as follows:

\widetilde{a}_{i}=\begin{cases}01&\text{ if }a_{i}\in\{00,01\}\\
10&\text{ if }a_{i}=10\end{cases}

The map
00\rightarrow 01
then supplies us with a map
\eta\colon\underline{a}\rightarrow\widetilde{\underline{a}}
. Since
\underline{a}\in B_{n}
, some of the
a_{i}
’s are either
00
or
01
, and so
\widetilde{\underline{a}}
indeed lies in
F_{n}
. Hence, we have an object
(\eta\colon\underline{a}\rightarrow\widetilde{\underline{a}})
in
(F_{n})_{\underline{a}/}
.

Now since we are dealing with a poset, to show that
\widetilde{\underline{a}}
is initial in
(F_{n})_{\underline{a}/}
and since
B_{n}\subseteq\prod_{n}\Lambda^{2}_{0}
is fully faithful, it suffices to show that
\map_{\prod_{n}\Lambda^{2}_{0}}(\widetilde{\underline{a}},\underline{f})\simeq\ast
for all
(\underline{a}\rightarrow\underline{f})\in(F_{n})_{\underline{a}/}
. For this, consider the map

\map_{\prod_{n}\Lambda^{2}_{0}}\big(\widetilde{\underline{a}},\underline{f}\big)\xlongrightarrow{\eta^{*}}\map_{\prod_{n}\Lambda^{2}_{0}}\big(\underline{a},\underline{f}\big)\simeq\ast

(21)

where the last term is contractible by definition of
(\underline{a}\rightarrow\underline{f})\in(F_{n})_{\underline{a}/}
. Now noting that
\map_{\prod_{n}\Lambda^{2}_{0}}(\underline{x},\underline{z})\simeq\prod_{i}\map_{\Lambda^{2}_{0}}(x_{i},z_{i})
, the map
Eq.

21
is easily seen to be an equivalence since
00\rightarrow 01
induces an equivalence
\map_{\Lambda^{2}_{0}}(01,01)\rightarrow\map_{\Lambda^{2}_{0}}(00,01)
.
∎

Corollary 3.2.6
.

The inclusion of
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories
\underline{F}_{f}\subseteq\underline{B}_{f}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–cofinal, and so restriction along this inclusion induces an equivalence
\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{B}_{f}}\simeq\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{F}_{f}}
.

Proof.

We may deduce this statement from the unparametrised
3.2.5
immediately since
{\mathcal{T}}
–cofinality may be checked fibrewise by
[
Sha23
, Thm. 6.7]
.
∎

Notation 3.2.7
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal category,
f\colon U\rightarrow V
a map in
{\mathcal{T}}
, and
(A\rightarrow B)=\varphi\colon\underline{\Delta}^{1}\rightarrow f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
a morphism in
f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. It will be convenient to use the notation
\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}_{f}}f_{\otimes}(A\rightarrow B)
for the
\underline{J}_{f}
–shaped colimit of the functor
\underline{J}_{f}\subseteq f_{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\xrightarrow{f_{*}\varphi}f_{*}f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\xrightarrow{f_{\otimes}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
.

We now come to the main proposition of this subsection:

Proposition 3.2.8
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–pointed category with all
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits equipped with a
{\mathcal{T}}
–distributive symmetric monoidal structure
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
. Let
f\colon U\rightarrow V
be a map in
{\mathcal{T}}
. If we have a cofibre sequence
A\rightarrow B\rightarrow C
in
f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
, then applying
f_{\otimes}
yields a cofibre sequence in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}

\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}_{f}}f_{\otimes}(A\rightarrow B)\longrightarrow f_{\otimes}B\longrightarrow f_{\otimes}C.

Proof.

We write
\partial\colon\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0}\rightarrow f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
for the diagram
(0\leftarrow A\rightarrow B)
for the diagram defining the cofibre
C
. Since
f_{\otimes}
was assumed to be distributive, we have a colimit diagram

\delta^{\underline{\triangleright}}\colon(f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0})^{\underline{\triangleright}}\longrightarrow f_{*}\big((\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0})^{\underline{\triangleright}}\big)\xlongrightarrow{f_{*}(\partial^{\underline{\triangleright}})}f_{*}f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\xlongrightarrow{f_{\otimes}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}

and so we obtain that
f_{\otimes}C
is the colimit of the diagram
\delta\colon f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. Now applying the colimit decomposition
2.2.10
on the pushout from
3.2.4
, we obtain the pushout diagram in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
(where we have suppressed the restriction functors for readability)
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}_{f}}\delta}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{M}_{f}}\delta}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{B}_{f}}\delta}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{\otimes}C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}

But then
\underline{M}_{f}
has a final object and the evaluation at the final object of the functor
\underline{M}_{f}\subseteq f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0}\xrightarrow{\delta}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
f_{\otimes}B
, hence we get
\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{M}_{f}}\delta\simeq f_{\otimes}B
. Next, by distributivity, tensoring with the zero object yields the zero object, and so since by definition
\underline{F}_{f}
contains at least one
01
in the tuples description from
3.2.3
, we see that the restricted functor
\underline{F}_{f}\subseteq f_{*}\underline{\Lambda}^{2}_{0}\xrightarrow{\delta}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
has constant value the zero object. Therefore, all in all, by
3.2.6
, we have that
\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{B}_{f}}\delta\simeq\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{F}_{f}}\delta\simeq 0
. Finally, by definition of our notation,
\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}_{f}}f_{\otimes}(A\rightarrow B)=\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}_{f}}\delta
. Combining all of these gives the claimed cofibre sequence.
∎

3.3
Special case of index 2 quotients in the equivariant setting

In preparation for our application to the algebraic K–theory of 2–groups in the next section, we will be considering the special case of
{\mathcal{T}}=\mathcal{O}_{G}
and where all parametrised colimits in sight come from an index 2 subgroup
H\leq G
. As we shall see, the special facts in the following observation conspire to make this situation particularly simple.

Observation 3.3.1
.

Let us collect all the elementary group theory we will need here. Let
H\leq G
be an index 2 subgroup and
K\leq G
be another subgroup.

1.

If the inclusion
H\cap K\leq K
is proper, then it is also an index 2 inclusion. This is because, fixing any
x\in K\backslash H
, we know by
|G/H|=2
that for any other
k\in K
,
k=xh
for some
h\in H
. But then
h=x^{-1}k\in K
and so
h\in H\cap K
, whence
|K/H\cap K|=2
.

2.

By the usual double coset decomposition, we know that
G/K\times G/H\cong\coprod_{g\in K\backslash G/H}G/H^{g}\cap K=\coprod_{g\in K\backslash G/H}G/H\cap K
where we have used that
H\leq G
was a normal subgroup since
|G/H|=2
. But then, again by
|G/H|=2
, there are only two possibilities for what the set
K\backslash G/H
can be, whence

G/K\times G/H=\begin{cases}(G/K)^{\coprod 2}&\text{ if }K\leq H\\
G/K\cap H&\text{ if }K\not\leq H\end{cases}

Proposition 3.3.2
.

Let
H\leq G
have index 2 and let
w\colon G/H\rightarrow G/G
be the unique map. In this case, the map
\varphi\colon(w_{!}w^{*}\underline{\ast})^{\underline{\triangleleft}}\hookrightarrow w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
from
3.1.5
induces via
3.1.4
an equivalence
\overline{\varphi}\colon((w_{!}w^{*}\underline{\ast})^{\underline{\triangleleft}})^{\underline{\triangleright}}\rightarrow w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
. Equivalently, in the notation of
3.2.3
, the map
\varphi
induces an equivalence
\varphi\colon(w_{!}w^{*}\underline{\ast})^{\underline{\triangleleft}}\xrightarrow{\simeq}\underline{J}_{w}
.

Proof.

Equivalences can be checked fibrewise, and so fixing a subgroup
K\leq G
and writing
r\colon G/K\rightarrow G/G
for the unique map, we will prove by induction on the order of
G
that

r^{*}\overline{\varphi}\colon r^{*}((w_{!}w^{*}\underline{\ast})^{\underline{\triangleleft}})^{\underline{\triangleright}}\simeq((r^{*}w_{!}w^{*}\underline{\ast})^{\underline{\triangleleft}})^{\underline{\triangleright}}\longrightarrow r^{*}w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}

(22)

is an equivalence. As the base case, the statement is vacuously true when
|G|=1
.

First suppose that
K\lneq G
. By the dichotomy in
3.3.1
(2), we have the two cases of pullbacks
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/K\coprod G/K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/H}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/H\cap K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/H}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/G}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/G}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i\sqcup gi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\sqcup\mathrm{id}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}

according as
K\leq H
or
K\not\leq H
. In the case
K\leq H
, we see that
r^{*}\psi\colon r^{*}w_{!}w^{*}\underline{\ast}\rightarrow r^{*}w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
is identified with the ordinary singleton inclusion

(i^{*}\sqcup i^{*}g^{*})w^{*}\underline{\ast}\simeq r^{*}\underline{\ast}\sqcup r^{*}\underline{\ast}\longrightarrow r^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\times r^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\simeq(i^{*}\times i^{*}g^{*})w^{*}\underline{\Delta}

since the map
\psi
was stable under basechange by
3.1.7
, and the map
r^{*}\underline{\ast}\sqcup r^{*}\underline{\ast}\rightarrow r^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\times r^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}
is the ordinary singleton inclusion by
Example

3.1.6
. Therefore, in this case we indeed have that
Eq.

22
is an equivalence. As for the case
K\not\leq H
, writing
z\colon G/H\cap K\rightarrow G/G
for the unique map, we have the identification of
r^{*}\psi
with

\psi\colon\ell_{!}z^{*}\underline{\ast}\longrightarrow\ell_{*}z^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}

again by stability of singleton inclusions with basechange
3.1.7
. But then by
3.3.1
(1) we know that
H\cap K\leq K
was an index 2 inclusion and
|K|<|G|
, and so by the inductive hypothesis,
Eq.

22
is also an equivalence, finishing the proof for this case.

Finally, for the case when
K=G
, we write
i\colon\{G/G\}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{G}^{\mathrm{op}}
for the inclusion. We would like to argue that applying
i^{*}
(which is the evaluation at
G/G
) to
\overline{\varphi}
gives an equivalence in
\mathrm{Cat}
. Now, we know that
i^{*}w_{*}w^{*}\underline{\Delta}^{1}\simeq\Delta^{1}
. On the other hand,
i^{*}w_{!}\underline{\ast}\simeq\emptyset
by
2.1.18
. Therefore, we see now that
i^{*}\overline{\varphi}
is identified with the map

(\emptyset^{\triangleleft})^{\triangleright}\longrightarrow\Delta^{1}

which is clearly an equivalence. This completes the inductive step and hence the proof of the proposition.
∎

4
Noncommutative motives and equivariant algebraic K–theory

In the final section, we put together all the general theory developed above to treat the parametrised version of algebraic K–theory. As with ordinary algebraic K–theory, the key notion is that of split Verdier sequences. Building upon the theory of
{{\mathcal{T}}}
–perfect-stable categories from
Section

2.5
, we shall introduce these sequences in the parametrised context in
Section

4.1
and deduce their properties from the unparametrised context via
2.5.11
. Using these sequences, we construct two variants of parametrised noncommutative motives
\underline{\mathrm{NMot}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{pw}}
and
\underline{\mathrm{NMot}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{nm}}
, called
pointwise
and
normed
motives, respectively. The former will be the one with a desirable universal property and which corepresents K–theory, whereas the latter will be the one that may be refined multiplicatively for formal reasons (c.f.
4.2.11
and
4.2.15
resp.
4.2.17
). Next, we shall employ the theory of parametrised cubes laid down in
Section

3
to show that these two types of motives coincide in the equivariant case when
G
is a 2–group, i.e.
|G|=2^{n}
for some
n
. The strategy is to show that additive functors satisfy descent against certain
C_{2}
–pushouts by transforming these diagrams into ordinary pushouts for which descent is known to be true. By a dévissage argument using the solvability of
p
–groups (which may be viewed as an equivariant replacement of “currying”), we then bootstrap the
C_{2}
–square descent to show in
4.3.11
that the two motives agree for arbitrary 2–groups. Finally, we combine this with
2.4.10
to treat the case of Swan K–theory in
Section

4.4
.

4.1

is

-semiadditive, and so

. Hence

preserves (co)fibre sequences and we have bifibre sequences in the three directions above. Furthermore,

∎

4.1.2

We learnt of the following observation from the forthcoming
[
CDH+
, Lem. 1.1.4]
, which was written in the more structured setting of Poincaré categories. We include the argument for
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}
here for the reader’s convenience.

Lemma 4.1.7
.

There is an adjunction
L:\func(\Delta^{1},\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})\rightleftarrows\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}:R
where
L({\mathcal{C}}\xrightarrow{f}{\mathcal{D}})\simeq{\mathcal{C}}\times_{{\mathcal{D}}}{\mathcal{D}}^{\Delta^{1}}
and
R({\mathcal{E}})\simeq(\mathcal{E}^{\Delta^{1}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{E}})
, where both
{\mathcal{D}}^{\Delta^{1}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{D}}
and
\mathcal{E}^{\Delta^{1}}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
are the target maps. Moreover, the right adjoint
R
preserves all colimits.

Proof.

To see that we have such an adjunction, we would like to construct an equivalence

\map_{\func(\Delta^{1},\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})}({\mathcal{C}}\xrightarrow{f}{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{E}^{\Delta^{1}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{tgt}}\mathcal{E})\simeq\map_{\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}}({\mathcal{C}}\times_{{\mathcal{D}}}{\mathcal{D}}^{\Delta^{1}},\mathcal{E})

(24)

natural in all the variables. For this, consider the split Verdier sequence

{\mathcal{D}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{C}}\times_{{\mathcal{D}}}{\mathcal{D}}^{\Delta^{1}}\twoheadrightarrow{\mathcal{C}}
classified by
{\mathcal{C}}\xrightarrow{f}{\mathcal{D}}
via
4.1.6
. Since the functor
\func^{\mathrm{ex}}(-,\mathcal{E})
preserves split Verdier sequences, we obtain another split Verdier sequence

\func^{\mathrm{ex}}({\mathcal{C}},\mathcal{E})\hookrightarrow\func^{\mathrm{ex}}({\mathcal{C}}\times_{{\mathcal{D}}}{\mathcal{D}}^{\Delta^{1}},\mathcal{E})\twoheadrightarrow\func^{\mathrm{ex}}({\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{E})

By the classification
4.1.6
yet again, we then obtain an equivalence

\func^{\mathrm{ex}}({\mathcal{C}}\times_{{\mathcal{D}}}{\mathcal{D}}^{\Delta^{1}},\mathcal{E})\simeq\func^{\mathrm{ex}}({\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{E})\times_{\func^{\mathrm{ex}}({\mathcal{C}},\mathcal{E})}\func^{\mathrm{ex}}({\mathcal{C}},\mathcal{E})^{\Delta^{1}}

Applying core groupoids
(-)^{\simeq}
to this yields the equivalence
Eq.

24
, which is clearly natural in all the inputs, as wanted. Finally, to see that the right adjoint preserves colimits, we just need to argue that the functor
(-)^{\Delta^{1}}
commutes with colimits. Using that
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}\simeq\mathrm{Pr}_{L,\mathrm{st},\omega}\simeq\mathrm{Pr}_{R,\mathrm{st},\omega\text{-filt}}^{\mathrm{op}}
and that the faithful inclusion
\mathrm{Pr}_{R,\mathrm{st},\omega\text{-filt}}\subset\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}
creates limits, we obtain

\mathrm{Ind}(\mathop{colim}\displaylimits_{j\in J}\mathcal{E}_{j})^{\Delta^{1}}\simeq(\mathop{colim}\displaylimits^{\mathrm{Pr}_{L}}_{j\in J}\mathrm{Ind}\mathcal{E}_{j})^{\Delta^{1}}\simeq(\lim^{\mathrm{Pr}_{R}}_{j\in J^{\mathrm{op}}}\mathrm{Ind}\mathcal{E}_{j})^{\Delta^{1}}\simeq\lim^{\mathrm{Pr}_{R}}_{j\in J^{\mathrm{op}}}(\mathrm{Ind}\mathcal{E}_{j})^{\Delta^{1}}\simeq\mathop{colim}\displaylimits_{j\in J}^{\mathrm{Pr}_{L}}\mathrm{Ind}(\mathcal{E}_{j})^{\Delta^{1}}

where the outer equivalences are by
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.3.5.15]
, whence the desired conclusion.
∎

By the preservation and reflection of fibrewise (co)limits from
2.5.11
, the right adjoint here also preserves all fibrewise colimits, and so in particular,
\kappa
–filtered colimits. Thus,
\underline{L}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
preserves
\kappa
-compact objects for all regular cardinals
\kappa
. Thus, if
(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\xrightarrow{f}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
is a
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-exact functor between
\kappa
-compact
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-perfect stable categories, then
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}{\times}_{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\Delta^{1}}
is
\kappa
-compact too.

Observation 4.1.11

(Waldhausen sequences)
.

Write
s\colon\Delta^{0}\rightarrow\Delta^{1}
and
t\colon\Delta^{0}\rightarrow\Delta^{1}
for the inclusion of the source and the target, respectively. One of Waldhausen’s many key original insights, translated in the parametrised setup, is the following: for

, then we have an equivalence of morphisms
F\beta\simeq F\alpha\oplus F\gamma\colon F\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow F\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
.

Proof.

The key for these kinds of statements is that both natural transformations

(\beta\Rightarrow\gamma),(\alpha\oplus\gamma\Rightarrow\gamma)\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\longrightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\Delta^{1}}

have the same fibres, i.e.
\alpha
. Hence, applying
F
and postcomposing further with the equivalence
F(\fib)\times F(t^{*})\colon F(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\Delta^{1}})\xrightarrow{\simeq}F(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\times F(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
from
4.1.11
yields that the two morphisms

F(\beta\Rightarrow\gamma),\>F(\alpha\oplus\gamma\Rightarrow\gamma)\colon F(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\longrightarrow F(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\Delta^{1}})

are equivalent. Finally, postcomposing now these two equivalent morphisms with
F(s^{*})\colon F(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\Delta^{1}})\rightarrow F(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
shows that we have an equivalence of morphisms

F(\beta)\simeq F(\alpha\oplus\gamma)\simeq F(\alpha)\oplus F(\gamma)\colon F(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\longrightarrow F(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})

as was to be shown.
∎

Remark 4.1.13
.

In fact, the proof of the second part of the lemma above shows that any additive functor already sends left–split or right–split Verdier sequences to fibre sequences.

We end this subsection by recording how stable valued additive functors interact with certain pushout diagrams. This will be needed in our analysis of equivariant algebraic K–theory when
G
is a 2–group in
Section

4.3
.

4.2
Two variants of noncommutative motives

In this section, we follow closely the methods of
[

.
But we also have the tautological equivalence
\underline{\func}^{L}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{\mathrm{NMot}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{pw},\mathrm{un}},\underline{\mathcal{E}})\simeq{\lim}_{\kappa}\underline{\func}^{L}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{\mathrm{NMot}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{pw},\mathrm{un},\kappa},\underline{\mathcal{E}})
. Therefore we can apply
4.2.7
to conclude.
∎

Construction 4.2.12

(Pointwise connective algebraic
\mathrm{K}
-theory)
.

Recall from
[
BGT13
]
that connective algebraic K-theory is given by the finite product-preserving functor

\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Q}_{\bullet}}\func(\mathbf{\Delta}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})\xrightarrow{(-)^{\simeq}}\func(\mathbf{\Delta}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{S})\xrightarrow{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}\mathcal{S}

where
\underline{\mathrm{Q}}_{n}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\simeq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\twistedArrow(\Delta^{n}),\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
, Quillen’s Q–construction. Since
\cmonoid(\mathcal{S})\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
preserves sifted colimits by
[
Lur17
,
\lx@sectionsign 3.2.3
]
, it in particular preserves geometric realisations. Hence the geometric realisation used above to define
\mathcal{K}
acquires a canonical commutative monoid structure because we have the factorisation
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cmonoid(\mathcal{S})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(-)^{\simeq}}

Thus we can apply the
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-cofree
2.1.5
and
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-semiadditivise to get

\underline{\mathcal{K}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{pw}}:\underline{\cmonoid}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})\longrightarrow\underline{\cmonoid}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathcal{S})

which we call the
pointwise parametrised algebraic K-theory space
. Levelwise, this looks like

\small\begin{split}\mackey_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathcal{K}):\>\>\func^{\times}(\effBurn({\mathcal{T}}),\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})&\xrightarrow{\underline{\mathrm{Q}}_{\bullet}}\func(\mathbf{\Delta}^{\mathrm{op}},\func^{\times}(\effBurn({\mathcal{T}}),\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}))\\
&\xrightarrow{(-)^{\simeq}}\func(\mathbf{\Delta}^{\mathrm{op}},\func^{\times}(\effBurn({\mathcal{T}}),\cmonoid(\mathcal{S})))\\
&\xrightarrow{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}\func^{\times}(\effBurn({\mathcal{T}}),\cmonoid(\mathcal{S}))\\
\end{split}\normalsize

We will have use of this description soon in analysing motivic suspensions. Note also that
\underline{\mathcal{K}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{pw}}
is an additive theory by the usual unparametrised additivity theorem and since we define split Verdier sequences in
\underline{\cmonoid}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})
as those that are pointwise split Verdier in the usual sense. Moreover, one can deloop the algebraic K-theory space
\mathcal{K}
to get an
algebraic K-theory spectrum

\mathrm{K}:\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}
which is the spectrum associated to the prespectrum whose
n
-th term is
\mathop{colim}\displaylimits_{\bullet\in(\mathbf{\Delta}^{\mathrm{op}})^{n}}(\mathrm{Q}_{\bullet}{\mathcal{C}})^{\simeq}
(cf.
[
BGT13
,
\lx@sectionsign 7.2
]
or Waldhausen’s original treatment
[
Wal85
]
for more details using the equivalent
\mathrm{S}_{\bullet}
–construction), and we write
\underline{\mathrm{K}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{pw}}
for the analogous pointwise K–theory spectrum. By construction, this fits into the commuting diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\uline{\phantom{$\displaystyle\mathrm{perf}$}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip .

Proof.

Since
\underline{\mathrm{Q}}_{n}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\simeq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\twistedArrow(\Delta^{n}),\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
, we get
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},\underline{\mathrm{Q}}_{n}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\simeq\underline{\mathrm{Q}}_{n}\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
from
2.1.9
(1). But then, both
\underline{\mathrm{Q}}_{n}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
and
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
inherit
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-(co)limits from
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
(the former by
2.1.9
(2)), and so clearly we obtain the statement required.
∎

sends split Verdier sequences to cofibre sequences by definition of unstable motives, and cofibre sequences are stable under colimits, we can apply
j_{\mathrm{un}}
to the simplicial split Verdier sequence and take geometric realisation in
\underline{\mathrm{NMot}}^{\mathrm{pw},\mathrm{un}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
to get a cofibre sequence in
\underline{\mathrm{NMot}}^{\mathrm{pw},\mathrm{un}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}

j_{\mathrm{un}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightarrow\mathop{colim}\displaylimits_{n\in\mathbf{\Delta}^{\mathrm{op}}}j_{\mathrm{un}}\underline{\mathrm{D\acute{e}c}}_{\bullet}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\mathop{colim}\displaylimits_{\bullet\in\mathbf{\Delta}^{\mathrm{op}}}j_{\mathrm{un}}\underline{\mathrm{Q}}_{\bullet}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}

But then we know that the middle term is always augmented over 0 and so is zero, hence the last term is a suspension of the first term, as required.
∎

We do not know in general if these comparison maps are equivalences. However, we are able to show that it
is
so in the case of equivariant algebraic K–theory for
G
a 2-group, and this is the content of the rest of the article.

3.

It might be tempting to try to prove directly that the map
\underline{\mathrm{K}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{pw}}\Rightarrow\underline{\mathrm{K}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{nm}}
is an equivalence by proving
4.2.15
in the case of normed motives. When one traces through this strategy, the key hiccup is in proving
4.2.14
that the Q–construction is already motivically local where we have used crucially that the parametrised algebraic K–theory space functor
\underline{\mathcal{K}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
is additive, i.e. that it interacts well with maps in
\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{pw}}
. What is needed in the normed setting is of course that it interacts well with maps in
\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{nm}}\supseteq\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{pw}}
. Indeed, as mentioned above, this is what we will show in the equivariant case for 2–groups in
Section

4.3
.

4.3
Pointwise K–theory is normed for 2-groups

In this subsection, we specialise the considerations of
Section

4.2
to the case of
{\mathcal{T}}=\mathcal{O}_{G}
where
G
is a finite group, giving
G
–equivariant algebraic K–theory. The end goal is to show
4.3.11
, which says that
\underline{\mathrm{K}}_{G}
refines to the structure of a normed ring
G
–spectrum when
G
is a 2–group. In other words, we will show that the comparison map

\Psi\colon\underline{\mathrm{NMot}}_{G}^{\mathrm{pw}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathrm{NMot}}_{G}^{\mathrm{nm}}\quad\text{ and hence also }\quad\underline{\mathrm{K}}_{G}^{\mathrm{pw}}\Longrightarrow\underline{\mathrm{K}}_{G}^{\mathrm{{nm}}}

from
4.2.19
(2) are equivalences. First, recall the notations
{\mathcal{U}}
and
\lambda
from
4.2.10
. Let us also take stock of the theory developed in
Section

3
in our current situation. While we have opted to use the more efficient stars and shrieks notation there, it would be beneficial now to switch to the more conventional notation in equivariant homotopy theory. We do this mainly because it is easier to keep track of the groups involved and because
C_{2}
–pushouts have an especially suggestive notation.

Notation 4.3.1
.

For a subgroup
H\leq G
and
w\colon G/H\rightarrow G/G
the unique map, we will from now on denote
w^{*},w_{!},w_{*}
by
\res^{G}_{H},\mathrm{Ind}^{G}_{H},\prod_{G/H}
respectively. In the presence of
G
–symmetric monoidal structures, we will write
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}
for
w_{\otimes}
. When
|G/H|=2
, we will write the colimit of the
C_{2}
–pushouts discussed in
Example

3.1.9
by
B\underline{\amalg}_{A}B
. In particular, by
3.2.2
in the case when
\underline{I}=w_{!}\underline{\ast}
, we may express
B\underline{\amalg}_{A}B
as the
ordinary
pushout
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Ind}^{G}_{H}\res^{G}_{H}A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Ind}^{G}_{H}B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\underline{\amalg}_{A}B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Ind}^{G}_{H}f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}

Finally, given a cofibre sequence
A\rightarrow B\rightarrow C
of
H
–objects in a pointed
G
–category with a
G
–distributive symmetric monoidal structure, a straightforward combination of
3.2.8
and
3.3.2
gives us a cofibre sequence of
G
–objects

A\otimes B\underline{\amalg}_{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}A}B\otimes A\longrightarrow\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}B\longrightarrow\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}C

We aim to prove that
\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{pw}}
is
\underline{\otimes}
–multiplicatively closed, i.e. if
H\leq G
and we have a split Verdier in

.

Corollary 4.3.2
.

Let
H\leq G
with
|G/H|=2
. Suppose we have a pushout
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}

\ulcorner

in a
G
–distributive symmetric monoidal
G
-stable category
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
.
Then we have the pushout
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes B\underline{\amalg}_{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}A}B\otimes A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\otimes Y\underline{\amalg}_{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}X}Y\otimes X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}Y}

\ulcorner

Proof.

Writing
C
for
\cofib(A\rightarrow B)\simeq\cofib(X\rightarrow Y)
, we get from the
G/H
-distributivity of
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}
together with
4.3.1
that we have the map of cofibre sequences
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes B\underline{\amalg}_{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}A}B\otimes A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\otimes Y\underline{\amalg}_{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}X}Y\otimes X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}C}

and so since
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
was stable, the left square is a fibrewise pushout.
∎

Next, recall the notion of saturation closure from
[
Hil22a
, Def. 6.3.5]
.

Observation 4.3.4
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be equipped with a
G
–distributive symmetric monoidal structure. Suppose that
S
were a tensor ideal, i.e. if for any
Z\in\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
and
f\colon A\rightarrow B
in
S
, we have that
\mathrm{id}_{Z}\otimes f
is also in
S
. Then by a standard argument, we know that
\overline{S}
is also a tensor ideal. To wit, consider the collection
U\subseteq\overline{S}
of morphisms
f
such that
\mathrm{id}_{Z}\otimes f
is again in
\overline{S}
for any
Z\in\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. By hypothesis on
S
, we know that
S\subseteq U
. Moreover, since
Z\otimes-
commutes with all colimits by
G
–distributivity of the symmetric monoidal structure, it is easy to see that the three axioms in
[
Hil22a
, Def. 6.3.5]
are satisfied so that
U
is a
G
–strongly saturated collection containing
S
, whence
U=\overline{S}
by minimality of
\overline{S}
.

Lemma 4.3.5
.

Let
H\leq G
with
|G/H|=2
and
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
a
G
–distributive symmetric monoidal
G
-stable category. Suppose
S
is a collection of morphisms in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
which is a tensor ideal and
\overline{S}
its
G
-strong saturation. If
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}
sends morphisms in
S
to morphisms in
\overline{S}
, then
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}
also preserves all morphisms in the saturation
\overline{S}
.

Proof.

Write
U\subseteq\overline{S}
for the collection of morphisms which get sent to a morphism in
\overline{S}
by
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}
. By hypothesis,
S\subseteq U
. We claim that
U
is
G
–strongly saturated. The 2-out-of-3 property is clear, and so we only have to check the first two axioms. To see axiom (2), we need to show that if
\partial:\underline{J}\rightarrow\underline{\func}_{H}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is a diagram that is pointwise in the full subcategory
\underline{\func}^{U}_{H}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
, then
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}}\partial\in\func_{G}^{\overline{S}}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}).
For this, recall by
G/H
-distributivity that
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{J}}\partial
is computed as the cone point of the
G
-colimit diagram

(\prod_{G/H}\underline{J})^{\underline{\triangleright}}\rightarrow\prod_{G/H}(\underline{J}^{\underline{\triangleright}})\xrightarrow{\prod_{G/H}\partial}\prod_{G/H}\underline{\func}_{H}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}}\underline{\func}_{G}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})

Now the hypothesis on
\partial
ensures that, when restricted to
\prod_{G/H}\underline{J}
, this composite lands in
\underline{\func}_{G}^{\overline{S}}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\subseteq\underline{\func}_{G}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
and since by definition
\underline{\func}_{G}^{\overline{S}}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is closed under
G
-colimits, we obtain that the cone point
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{J}\partial
is indeed in
\underline{\func}_{G}^{\overline{S}}(\Delta^{1},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
as required.

Finally, to see axiom (3), suppose we have a pushout of
H
–objects in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}

\ulcorner

where the left vertical is in
U
(and so, by definition of saturation, the right vertical is in
\overline{S}
). Then by
4.3.2
we obtain the pushout square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes B\underline{\amalg}_{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}A}B\otimes A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\otimes Y\underline{\amalg}_{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}X}Y\otimes X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}Y}

\ulcorner

(26)

Hence if we can show that the left vertical map is in
\overline{S}
, then by definition, the right vertical map will be in
\overline{S}
too. For this, by
4.3.1
we have
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Ind}^{G}_{H}\res^{G}_{H}\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Ind}^{G}_{H}(A\otimes B)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes B\underline{\amalg}_{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}A}A\otimes B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon}

\ulcorner

and similarly for
X\otimes Y\underline{\amalg}_{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}X}X\otimes Y
. Since the respective maps on the upper three terms between the ones for the pair
(A,B)
and the ones for the pair
(X,Y)
are all in
\overline{S}
by hypothesis (the bottom left uses that
\overline{S}
is a tensor ideal by
4.3.4
), so is the induced map
A\otimes B\underline{\amalg}_{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}A}A\otimes B\rightarrow X\otimes Y\underline{\amalg}_{\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}X}X\otimes Y
by axiom (2) of
[
Hil22a
, Def. 6.3.5]
. Therefore, the pushout
Eq.

26
gives that
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}B\rightarrow\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}Y
is also in
\overline{S}
as required.
∎

Lemma 4.3.6
.

Let
H\leq G
with
|G/H|=2
and
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
a
G
–distributive symmetric monoidal
G
-stable category. Let
T
be a collection of morphisms and
S\supseteq T
the smallest tensor ideal containing
T
. If
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}
sends morphisms in
T
to morphisms in
\overline{S}
, then
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}
also preserves all morphisms in
\overline{S}
.

Proof.

By
4.3.5
, it suffices to show that
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}
sends morphisms in
S
to
\overline{S}
. So let
U\subseteq S
be the collection of morphisms which get sent to
\overline{S}
under
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}
. By hypothesis, this contains
T
, and it is easy to check that it is also a tensor ideal because
\overline{S}
is again a tensor ideal by
4.3.4
. Hence by minimality we see that
U=S
as required.
∎

.

The final ingredient to the main theorem is the following standard fact in group theory.

Proposition 4.3.10
.

Let
p
be a prime,
G
be a p-group, and
H\leq G
a subgroup. There is a normal series
H=N_{0}\triangleleft N_{1}\triangleleft\cdots\triangleleft N_{k}=G
such that the quotients
N_{m}/N_{m-1}\cong C_{p}
for all
m
.

Proof.

If
H\leq G
is itself already normal, then this is immediate since we can just obtain this from the
C_{p}
-solvability of the
p
-group
G/H
. Suppose
H\leq G
is a proper subgroup. We claim that we have the proper inclusion
H\lneq\mathrm{N}_{H}G
into the normaliser: given this, we can now induct by taking successive normalisers and applying the statement in the case of
H\leq G
being normal. To see the claim, consider the left action of
H
on the left
H
-cosets of
G
. Since
H
fixes the coset
H
, this action has a point with singleton orbit, and so since everything in sight are
p
-groups, we get from the orbit-stabiliser theorem that there is another
H
-coset
gH
, for some
g\in G\backslash H
, fixed by the left
H
–action. This means that for all
h\in H
, we get that
hgH=gH
, so that
g\in G\backslash H
is a normaliser of
H
which is not in
H
, as asserted.
∎

Theorem 4.3.11
.

Let
G
be a 2-group. The inclusion
\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{pw},\kappa}\subseteq\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{nm},\kappa}
is an identification, and hence the comparison
\Psi:\underline{\mathrm{NMot}}_{G}^{\mathrm{pw}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathrm{NMot}}_{G}^{\mathrm{nm}}
from
4.2.19
is an equivalence.

Proof.

Let
H\leq G
be a subgroup. We need to show that
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}
preserves
{\lambda}
-equivalences. Equivalently, by
[
Hil22a
, Prop. 6.3.6]
, we need to show
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}
preserves morphisms in
\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{pw}}
, the
G
-strong saturation of
\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{pw}}=\langle\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\xrightarrow{s_{*}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\Delta^{1}}\xrightarrow{t^{*}}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rangle
. By
4.3.10
, let
H=N_{0}\triangleleft N_{1}\triangleleft\cdots\triangleleft N_{k}=G
be a
C_{2}
-normal series. Since
\mathrm{N}^{G}_{H}\simeq\mathrm{N}^{N_{k}}_{N_{k-1}}\circ\cdots\circ\mathrm{N}^{N_{1}}_{N_{0}}
, it would suffice to show that
\mathrm{N}^{N_{m}}_{N_{m-1}}
preserves morphisms in
\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{pw}}
. But then
N_{m-1}\triangleleft N_{m}
is a normal inclusion of index 2, and so this assertion is true by
4.3.9
.
∎

In view of
4.2.19
, the following is now an immediate consequence of the theorem.

2.

By the last statement in
4.4.2
, any symmetric monoidal perfect–stable
{\mathcal{C}}^{\otimes}
equipped with a symmetric monoidal
G
–action gives rise to a collection of spectra
\big\{{\mathrm{K}}({\mathcal{C}}^{hH})\big\}_{H\leq G}
which canonically assemble to a
G
–normed ring spectrum.
